title: Flexible Rigidity: Compiling Generic Trusted-preparation Protocols Into Sequential Device-independent Protocols
authors: Amir Arqand, Srijita Kundu, Ernest Y. -Z. Tan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a generic compiler for turning a wide class of device-dependent protocols with trusted state preparation into sequential device-independent protocols. In order for our compiler to apply, the trusted-preparation protocol needs to satisfy certain minimal conditions: having an entanglement-based realization in the first place, and the entanglement-based realization corresponding to the optimal strategy of any non-local game that satisfies a fairly weak rigidity condition. We apply our generic compiler to give sequential device-independent protocols for uncloneable encryption, copy-protection of point functions, and blind randomness expansion. Our technical contribution is a new class of rigidity theorems based on R\'{e}nyi divergences, with flexible cryptographic applications. They allow our compiler to achieve a constant rate (i.e., the ratio of trusted states prepared to device uses), while tolerating a constant level of noise per device usage. This overcomes a fundamental scaling obstacle faced by previous rigidity theorems for trace distance or fidelity. For the generic sequential case, our proof is based on the sharp-divergence chain rule by Fawzi and Fawzi (2021), which suffices for a constant but fairly low rate. In the special case when the devices retain no memory, we improve the rates by deriving a novel subadditivity property for a modified channel sandwiched divergence, which may be of independent interest. Finally, as a prospect for future improvements, we also prove a chain rule for the iterated-mean divergences from Brown, Fawzi and Fawzi (2021).
tldr: The paper introduces a generic compiler that turns trusted-preparation device-dependent protocols into sequential device-independent protocols using new Rényi-divergence-based rigidity theorems.
motivation: Previous rigidity theorems based on trace distance or fidelity cannot achieve constant rate under constant noise, creating a fundamental scaling obstacle for device-independent protocols.
method: The authors develop rigidity theorems based on Rényi divergences and use the sharp-divergence chain rule of Fawzi and Fawzi, plus a novel subadditivity property for memoryless devices, to compile trusted-preparation protocols into sequential device-independent ones.
result: The compiler yields sequential device-independent protocols for uncloneable encryption, copy-protection of point functions, and blind randomness expansion, achieving constant rate while tolerating constant noise per device use.
conclusion: Flexible rigidity via Rényi divergences overcomes previous scaling limits and enables efficient device-independent cryptography, with a chain rule for iterated-mean divergences suggested for future improvements.

title: Entanglement Cost Of Quantum Depolarization
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement cost is the asymptotic rate of Bell pairs required to prepare a quantum state. Its regularized definition has made exact evaluation difficult, even for isotropic states (i.e., depolarized maximally entangled states). In this work, we determine the entanglement cost of every qubit isotropic state and, more generally, every two-qubit Bell-diagonal state. Our proof uses a family of suitably tuned qubit semigroups to transform a general log-Sobolev entropy bound into supporting lines of Wootters' function. A recent exact tensorization theorem of Dong et al. [arXiv:2606.17729] extends these bounds to arbitrarily many copies, yielding a general lower bound on entanglement cost. Matching this bound with the entanglement of formation also determines the exact cost for a broader class of two-qubit states. For qudit isotropic states, we derive another general lower bound from the full depolarizing [MATH] norm. This bound substantially improves on the PPT-relative entropy of entanglement and nearly matches the entanglement of formation, leaving a gap of at most [MATH] of [MATH] that vanishes as [MATH] grows. Finally, the exact qubit results and qudit bounds extend to the entanglement cost of preparing quantum depolarizing channels under both parallel and sequential strategies.
tldr: The paper determines the exact entanglement cost for all qubit isotropic states and two-qubit Bell-diagonal states, and gives improved lower bounds for qudit isotropic states and quantum depolarizing channels.
motivation: Entanglement cost is a fundamental entanglement measure, but its regularized definition makes exact evaluation difficult even for highly symmetric states such as isotropic states.
method: The proof uses tuned qubit semigroups to convert a log-Sobolev entropy bound into supporting lines of Wootters' function, combined with an exact tensorization theorem to extend the bound to arbitrarily many copies.
result: The exact entanglement cost is obtained for every qubit isotropic state and every two-qubit Bell-diagonal state; for qudit isotropic states, a lower bound from the depolarizing norm nearly matches the entanglement of formation, with a gap vanishing as the dimension grows.
conclusion: These results also extend to the entanglement cost of preparing quantum depolarizing channels under both parallel and sequential strategies, resolving a long-standing open problem for qubit isotropic states.

title: Quantum Key Distribution Using Generalized Contextuality Against Post-quantum Eavesdroppers
authors: Daniel Centeno, Roberto D. Baldij\~{a}o, Maria Ciudad Ala\~n\'on, Yujie Zhang, Pedro Lauand, Elie Wolfe
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bell nonlocality allows secret key to be certified without trusting the internal operation of the devices, and even against eavesdroppers constrained only by the no-signaling principle. We ask whether generalized contextuality, a notion of nonclassicality available in prepare-and-measure experiments on a single system, can play an analogous role. In our approach, Alice and Bob first establish operational equivalences among their local preparation and measurement procedures, which are then treated as theory-independent constraints that any physical intervention on the communication channel, including that of an adversary, must respect. Eve is otherwise unrestricted, that is, her intervention on the transmitted system is not assumed to be described by quantum theory. Within this adversarial model, we show that Eve's optimal guessing probability against individual attacks is the solution of a finite linear program, and hence that a worst-case asymptotic key rate follows from the observed statistics and the operational equivalences alone. We prove that contextuality is necessary for a positive key rate. However, we also show that it is not sufficient. Concretely, the (3,2)-parity-oblivious random access code, known to yield secret key against a quantum eavesdropper, yields none certifiable key rate against a post-quantum one. Conversely, operational equivalences with no analogue among no-signaling constraints can strictly increase the asymptotic key rate. We illustrate this with the prepare-and-measure version of the standard CHSH protocol with an aligned key-generating setting.
tldr: The paper shows that generalized contextuality in prepare-and-measure experiments can certify quantum key distribution even against post-quantum eavesdroppers, deriving key rates from operational equivalences and proving contextuality is necessary but not sufficient.
motivation: Bell nonlocality enables device-independent key distribution, but it requires entanglement and no-signaling constraints. The authors ask whether generalized contextuality, available in single-system prepare-and-measure setups, can play an analogous role for QKD against adversaries not restricted to quantum theory.
method: Alice and Bob establish operational equivalences among their preparations and measurements, treating these as theory-independent constraints on any physical intervention by Eve. Eve's optimal guessing probability under individual attacks is computed as a finite linear program, yielding an asymptotic key rate from observed statistics and operational equivalences alone.
result: Contextuality is necessary for a positive key rate but not sufficient: the (3,2)-parity-oblivious random access code certifies no key against a post-quantum eavesdropper despite being secure against a quantum one. Conversely, operational equivalences without no-signaling analogues can strictly increase the key rate, illustrated with a prepare-and-measure CHSH protocol.
conclusion: Generalized contextuality provides a novel route to semi-device-independent QKD robust against post-quantum adversaries, though the sufficiency of contextuality for key generation is limited and depends on the specific operational equivalences.

title: Quantum Secret Sharing And Error Correction Vs No-Cloning
authors: Steven Chien, Ishani Mukherjee, Mark Zhandry
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Secret sharing is ubiquitous throughout cryptography. All possible access structures are classically feasible, and in the case of threshold access structures, the protocols are even very efficient. However, when moving to the quantum setting, the no-cloning theorem shows that many access structures are impossible. In fact, no-cloning exactly characterizes feasibility: for thresholds, quantum secret sharing is possible if and only if the threshold [MATH] is strictly more than [MATH]. In this work, we propose a variant of quantum secret sharing (QSS) where two or more identical copies of the input state are provided, but the output is only required to recover one copy. This notion circumvents the simple one-copy no-cloning obstruction, though the natural [MATH]-copy generalization still gives much milder obstructions. For thresholds using [MATH] copies, no-cloning implies that QSS is impossible whenever [MATH]. It is tempting to hypothesize that no-cloning continues to exactly characterize the many-copy case. However, we show that this is not the case. We give positive results showing that multiple copies allow for going slightly beyond the single-copy obstruction: for thresholds, we construct QSS whenever [MATH]. On the other hand, we give a novel obstruction we call the Clique Path obstruction, which applies to arbitrary access structures. For thresholds, it shows that QSS is impossible whenever [MATH]. Our upper and lower bounds exactly match for [MATH]. Both our results leverage connections to the [MATH]-colorability of certain graphs derived from the access structure. We leave closing the gap for [MATH] copies as a fascinating direction for future work. Secret sharing is closely related to error correction, which can also be considered in the many-copy setting. Our results imply similar obstructions for quantum error correction for erasure channels.
tldr: The paper studies many-copy quantum secret sharing and shows that no-cloning does not fully characterize feasibility, giving matching bounds for two copies and a new Clique Path obstruction.
motivation: Quantum secret sharing is fundamentally limited by the no-cloning theorem, and understanding whether providing multiple input copies can circumvent this obstruction is important for quantum cryptography and error correction.
method: The authors introduce a multi-copy variant of quantum secret sharing where several identical input states are provided but only one copy must be recovered, and they connect feasibility to graph colorability derived from the access structure.
result: They construct QSS schemes beyond the single-copy no-cloning bound and prove a novel Clique Path obstruction; for two copies the upper and lower bounds exactly match, and the results imply analogous obstructions for quantum error correction against erasure.
conclusion: No-cloning does not exactly characterize many-copy quantum secret sharing, and closing the gap for more than two copies remains an open direction.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a many-copy variant of quantum secret sharing (QSS) where the dealer provides k identical copies of the secret state, but the reconstruction only needs to recover one copy. The motivation is to circumvent the no-cloning obstruction that limits standard single-copy QSS: for threshold access structures, single-copy QSS is possible iff t > n/2. With k copies, the natural no-cloning bound becomes t > n/(k+1). The authors show that this bound is not tight: they construct protocols achieving QSS for thresholds whenever t > (n-k+1)/2, and they prove a new impossibility result, the Clique Path obstruction, which for thresholds implies impossibility when t ≤ (n-1)/k. For k=2, these bounds match exactly, giving a complete characterization: QSS is possible iff t > (n-1)/2. The results are derived by connecting QSS to the k-colorability of certain graphs derived from the access structure. The paper also notes implications for quantum error correction against erasure errors in the many-copy setting.

The positive result is achieved by designing explicit quantum secret sharing schemes that leverage multiple copies to distribute shares according to the access structure, using techniques from quantum error correction and graph coloring. The impossibility result, the Clique Path obstruction, is proven by reducing the existence of a QSS scheme to a graph coloring problem: if the graph derived from the access structure is not k-colorable, then no k-copy QSS scheme can exist. This reduction allows the authors to apply combinatorial arguments to derive threshold bounds. The matching bounds for k=2 are obtained by showing that the graph coloring condition is both necessary and sufficient in that case. The methodology is rigorous and combines quantum information theory with combinatorial graph theory.

The paper does not provide explicit numerical examples beyond the threshold formulas, but the bounds are tight for k=2.

title: Physical-Work Fluctuation Relations From Accessible Quantum Macrostates
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00246v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Jarzynski's equality recovers an equilibrium free-energy difference from nonequilibrium work trajectories, but its exponential average can converge very slowly because rare trajectories carry large weight. We show that coarse thermodynamic information measured at the nonequilibrium endpoint can reduce this sampling burden while keeping the same microscopic trajectories and the same free-energy target. The endpoint mean energy and a coarse spatial record define a maximum-entropy state and select one member of an exact family of fluctuation relations. title: When Information Is Not Enough: Accuracy-Constrained Thermodynamic Costs Of Binary Classification
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00291v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much entropy must a physical classifier produce to achieve a prescribed accuracy? Rate--distortion theory specifies the minimum information required, but does that information threshold suffice to determine the physical cost? We show that it does not, even for a binary task and a two-state memory. For a uniform binary target observed through a finite symmetric experiment, replacing the classification-error constraint with its necessary mutual-information threshold strictly lowers the infimum of entropy production under a common operation time, integrated mobility budget, and sufficiently large finite transition-rate cap. The separation holds whenever the target error lies strictly between the Bayes error of the observations and chance. Two results establish this physical gap. First, ordering observations by posterior confidence gives exact transport--risk and transport--information frontiers. Observations with the same Bayes error can have different cost frontiers. Second, we construct bounded-rate protocols that realize prescribed encoders with write probabilities below one, starting from exact reset, with an explicit excess cost above the transport bound. An achievable information-constrained cost then falls below a lower bound valid for every task-feasible protocol. Examples with repeated noisy observations illustrate the separation. The results identify a limitation of information-only benchmarks for physical classification: task accuracy and kinetic constraints must be retained explicitly. The cost analyzed is total entropy production during memory writing, excluding data acquisition, controller operation, and subsequent reset.
tldr: For binary classification with a two-state memory, the mutual-information threshold alone does not determine the minimum entropy production; accuracy and kinetic constraints must be retained explicitly.
motivation: Rate-distortion theory specifies the minimum information needed for a prescribed accuracy, but it is unclear whether that information threshold suffices to determine the physical thermodynamic cost of a classifier.
method: The paper analyzes a uniform binary target observed through a finite symmetric experiment, derives exact transport-risk and transport-information frontiers ordered by posterior confidence, and constructs bounded-rate protocols realizing prescribed encoders with write probabilities below one.
result: Replacing the classification-error constraint with its necessary mutual-information threshold strictly lowers the infimum entropy production under common operation time, integrated mobility budget, and finite transition-rate cap, whenever the target error lies between the Bayes error and chance.
conclusion: Information-only benchmarks are insufficient for physical classification; task accuracy and kinetic constraints must be kept explicit, as the cost of memory writing excludes data acquisition, controller operation, and reset.

They compare two optimization problems: one that constrains the classification error directly, and another that replaces the error constraint with its necessary mutual-information threshold. Under a common operation time, integrated mobility budget, and a sufficiently large finite transition-rate cap, they prove that the infimum of entropy production is strictly lower when using the information constraint. This separation occurs whenever the target error lies strictly between the Bayes error of the observations and chance (0.5). Thus, information alone is not a sufficient proxy for physical cost.

To establish this gap, the authors derive two key results. First, they show that ordering observations by posterior confidence yields exact transport–risk and transport–information frontiers. This means that observations with identical Bayes error can have different cost frontiers, implying that the Bayes error alone does not determine the minimal entropy production. Second, they construct bounded-rate protocols that realize prescribed encoders with write probabilities below one, starting from exact reset, and quantify the excess cost above the transport bound. They then demonstrate an achievable information-constrained cost that falls below a lower bound valid for every task-feasible protocol. This proves that the information-constrained infimum is strictly smaller than the task-constrained infimum. The results are illustrated with examples involving repeated noisy observations.

The paper concludes that information-only benchmarks are insufficient for physical classification; task accuracy and kinetic constraints must be retained explicitly. title: A Frame-Spread Lower Bound For Quantum Entropy Estimation Under Fixed Rank-One Measurements
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study estimation of the von Neumann entropy of a [MATH]-dimensional quantum state from independent outcomes of a fixed rank-one measurement. Let [MATH] denote the normalized trace-zero frame spread; [MATH] for exact complex projective [MATH]-designs. For any fixed rank-one measurement and [MATH], the minimax mean-squared error is at least [MATH]. For bounded frame spread and every fixed [MATH], the minimax risk is of order [MATH] throughout [MATH]; hence fixed uniform accuracy requires [MATH] observations. Existing tomography bounds give bounded risk from [MATH] observations for finite equal-weight exact designs and the Haar covariant measurement, while the intermediate minimax regime remains open. The results concern a fixed measurement repeated independently across copies; adaptive and collective protocols, and protocols that reuse common randomness across copies, are not covered.
tldr: The paper establishes a frame-spread lower bound on the minimax mean-squared error for estimating von Neumann entropy from fixed rank-one measurements, yielding sample-complexity requirements for uniform accuracy.
motivation: Estimating quantum entropy is fundamental to quantum information, yet sample-complexity lower bounds for practical fixed measurements remain less understood than those for full tomography or covariant designs.
method: It analyzes minimax risk for von Neumann entropy estimation using independent outcomes of a fixed rank-one measurement, introducing the normalized trace-zero frame spread and leveraging complex projective designs and information-theoretic lower bounds.
result: For any fixed rank-one measurement and dimension, the minimax MSE is at least proportional to the frame spread; for bounded frame spread, the minimax risk scales as 1/N, so fixed uniform accuracy requires Θ(1/ε²) observations, while existing tomography bounds cover only special designs.
conclusion: The work provides a general lower bound for nonadaptive entropy estimation under fixed rank-one measurements and highlights an open intermediate minimax regime, excluding adaptive, collective, or common-randomness-assisted protocols.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper studies the problem of estimating the von Neumann entropy of an unknown d-dimensional quantum state from n independent copies, where each copy is measured by a fixed rank-one measurement (i.e., a fixed orthonormal basis or, more generally, a fixed rank-one POVM). The central quantity is the normalized trace-zero frame spread κ_ν ∈ [1, d+1], which measures how far the measurement is from being an exact complex projective 2-design; κ_ν = 1 for exact 2-designs. The main result is a minimax lower bound on the mean-squared error: for any fixed rank-one measurement and n ≤ c₂ d²/κ_ν, the minimax MSE is at least c₁ log²(d²/(κ_ν n)). Consequently, for bounded frame spread and any fixed 0 < a < 2, the minimax risk remains of order log² d throughout the regime n ≲ d^{2-a}, implying that achieving fixed uniform accuracy requires Ω(d²) observations. The authors contrast this with existing upper bounds from quantum state tomography, which give bounded risk from O(d³ log³ d) observations for finite equal-weight exact designs and the Haar covariant measurement, leaving the intermediate minimax regime open. The results apply to protocols where the same fixed measurement is repeated independently on each copy; adaptive, collective, and common-randomness-reusing protocols are explicitly excluded.
key_contributions: Introduces the normalized trace-zero frame spread κ_ν as a quantitative measure of how close a rank-one measurement is to an exact complex projective 2-design, with κ_ν ∈ [1, d+1] and κ_ν = 1 for exact 2-designs.
Establishes a minimax lower bound of the form c₁ log²(d²/(κ_ν n)) on the MSE for entropy estimation from n independent outcomes of any fixed rank-one measurement, valid for n ≤ c₂ d²/κ_ν.
Shows that for bounded frame spread, the minimax risk is Θ(log² d) throughout n ≲ d^{2-a} for any fixed a < 2, implying that Ω(d²) observations are necessary for fixed uniform accuracy.
Compares the lower bound with known tomography upper bounds (O(d³ log³ d) for exact designs and Haar covariant measurements), identifying an open intermediate regime.
Clarifies the scope of the results by excluding adaptive, collective, and common-randomness-reusing protocols, thereby delineating the boundary of the established minimax theory.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs minimax decision-theoretic techniques to derive lower bounds on the mean-squared error for von Neumann entropy estimation. The key technical tool is the normalized trace-zero frame spread κ_ν, which quantifies the deviation of a rank-one measurement from an exact complex projective 2-design. The authors likely use information-theoretic arguments, such as Le Cam's method or Fano's inequality, combined with properties of the frame spread, to construct a lower bound that depends on the number of copies n and the dimension d. The analysis focuses on non-adaptive, non-collective protocols where the same measurement is applied independently to each copy, and the bound is expressed in terms of the log² of the effective sample size d²/(κ_ν n). The derivation appears to leverage the fact that for n below a threshold proportional to d²/κ_ν, the measurement outcomes do not provide enough information to distinguish states with different entropies, leading to a logarithmic-squared lower bound. The comparison with tomography upper bounds suggests a gap that is not resolved by the current techniques.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main quantitative result is the minimax lower bound: for any fixed rank-one measurement and n ≤ c₂ d²/κ_ν, the MSE is at least c₁ log²(d²/(κ_ν n)). This implies that when κ_ν is bounded (e.g., for exact 2-designs where κ_ν = 1), the risk remains of order log² d for all n up to d^{2-a} for any fixed a < 2. In particular, achieving a fixed uniform accuracy requires at least Ω(d²) observations. The gap between Ω(d²) and O(d³ log³ d) leaves an intermediate regime open, which the authors highlight as an open problem. The result is notable because it shows that even with an optimal fixed measurement (e.g., an exact 2-design), entropy estimation is fundamentally hard in the low-sample regime, requiring quadratically many samples in d to achieve constant accuracy.

The constants c₁ and c₂ are not specified, and the bound is asymptotic in d, so finite-dimensional behavior is not quantified.

title: Blind Unforgeability Implies Plus-One Unforgeability
authors: Mehil Agarwal, Calliope S. Reimann, Fang Song
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00517v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that quantum blind-unforgeability implies quantum plus-one unforgeability, settling an open question in the literature. Since plus-one unforgeability is known not to imply blind-unforgeability, our result establishes that blind-unforgeability is than plus-one unforgeability in the quantum setting. The implication is proven using a new technique that coherently rescales the query histories of a quantum-query algorithm in a black-box manner. This enables us to transform any successful plus-one attacker into a blind-unforgeability attacker with only inverse-polynomial loss. Our proof represents a conceptual shift from merely extracting a useful query history as in earlier attempts, which we show inevitably fails in general, to first coherently reshaping how query histories interfere.
tldr: The paper proves that quantum blind-unforgeability implies quantum plus-one unforgeability, resolving an open question and establishing a strict hierarchy of quantum security notions.
motivation: Plus-one unforgeability is known not to imply blind-unforgeability, but whether the converse holds in the quantum setting was open. Establishing the implication clarifies the relative strength of these cryptographic security notions.
method: The authors introduce a new proof technique that coherently rescales the query histories of a quantum-query algorithm in a black-box manner, transforming any successful plus-one attacker into a blind-unforgeability attacker with only inverse-polynomial loss.
result: They show that blind-unforgeability is strictly stronger than plus-one unforgeability in the quantum setting, and demonstrate that earlier proof attempts based solely on extracting useful query histories cannot work in general.
conclusion: The work settles the open question by shifting from classical query-history extraction to coherently reshaping how query histories interfere, providing a new tool for quantum cryptographic reductions.

title: Mixed-state Phases Induced By Power-law Quantum Channels
authors: Christopher Fechisin, Tsung-Cheng Lu, Zhi-Yuan Wei, Jeet Shah, Yu-Xin Wang, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Cheng-Ju Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00480v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open quantum systems can exhibit inherently mixed quantum orders, such as strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SW-SSB), which have no analogue in pure states. It is generally expected that a finite-depth local quantum channel cannot induce a phase transition to SW-SSB in one spatial dimension. We circumvent this obstruction by introducing a long-range quantum channel, which implements two-body dephasing on pairs of sites with probability falling off according to a power-law in the site separation. Applying this channel to a one-parameter family of matrix product states interpolating between trivial and symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases, we construct a phase diagram that hosts trivial, mixed SPT, and SW-SSB phases with respect to R\'enyi-2 diagnostics. Notably, the mixed SPT phase is distinct from previously studied decohered SPT phases: it hosts two logical qubits and exhibits nonvanishing R\'enyi-2 string order, despite vanishing conventional string order. Through a series of mappings to a classical statistical mechanics model, we establish a direct connection between the loss of logical information and the onset of SW-SSB in this model. Finally, we consider the feasibility of experimental realization of the phenomena we have studied. We emphasize that our family of mixed states can be tuned to regimes of high purity, substantially reducing measurement overhead and enabling their experimental realization and detection on near-term quantum hardware.

A factor code is defined by an isometry T: H_code → H_phys together with a unital *-homomorphism φ: B(H_code) → B(H_phys) satisfying φ(O)T = T O for all logical operators O. The unital condition is possible exactly when dim H_code divides dim H_phys, in which case φ(B(H_code)) is a von Neumann factor subalgebra of B(H_phys). The authors then consider a network of Hilbert spaces indexed by a partially ordered set, with isometries T_ji: H_i → H_j for i < j satisfying the composition rule T_kj T_ji = T_ki. The central question is when such a code network can be 'promoted' to a factor code network by choosing unital operator maps φ_ji such that (T_ji, φ_ji) is a factor code and the maps compose: φ_kj φ_ji = φ_ki.

The main results characterize the conditions for promotion. For networks with a tree structure, the divisibility conditions on Hilbert space dimensions are sufficient. However, for a diamond-shaped network (four nodes with i1, i2 < j and a common lower node), promotion is possible if and only if the principal angles between the subspaces T_42 H_2 and T_43 H_3 all have multiplicities divisible by dim H_1. The paper also provides a detailed characterization of the relative commutant structure for incomparable nodes: for i1, i2 < j, it determines when φ_{j i1}(B(H_{i1})) and φ_{j i2}(B(H_{i2})) commute, when they generate all of B(H_j), and when their intersection is trivial (only multiples of the identity). Furthermore, for i < j1, j2 < k, it characterizes when the intersection of the images of B(H_{j1}) and B(H_{j2}) equals the image of B(H_i), and when these algebras together with B(H_k) form a nondegenerate commuting square.

The results have implications for the structure of quantum error-correcting codes, especially in the context of topological quantum codes and holographic duality, where such networks naturally arise.

For spin [MATH] one scalar governs the loss, the packet average [MATH] of [MATH] (where [MATH] is the Wigner angle); for any spin, a ray degrades at a rate set by its spin variance transverse to the boost. In the spin-only account, the Free Will Theorem's SPIN axiom fails for every [MATH]; the Yu-Oh set loses contextuality between [MATH] and [MATH], with state independence going first; the Peres-Mermin square loses contextuality at [MATH] or [MATH] by orientation; singlet CHSH loses nonlocality for [MATH]; and a GHZ-state OR gate loses Raussendorf's contextuality certificate at [MATH]. A [MATH]-plate implements the channel exactly on photon polarisation, with a retardation in place of the rapidity, so the nonlocality, GHZ and aimed-source results are testable without motion.
tldr: The paper shows that Kochen-Specker contextuality is not Lorentz invariant when restricted to spin degrees of freedom, as momentum-dependent Wigner rotations make spin observables unsharp and break contextuality certificates.
motivation: To determine whether fundamental quantum nonclassicality, such as Kochen-Specker contextuality and Bell nonlocality, is frame-independent in relativistic settings.
method: The authors compare boosts on the full Hilbert space with spin-only subspaces, derive how Wigner rotations dephase spin observables, and evaluate the impact on Yu-Oh, Peres-Mermin, CHSH, GHZ, and the Free Will Theorem's SPIN axiom, proposing a waveplate-based optical simulation.
result: Contextuality and nonlocality degrade under boosts: state-independent contextuality is lost first, Peres-Mermin loses contextuality at specific orientations, singlet CHSH loses nonlocality, and the GHZ contextuality certificate vanishes for certain boosts.
conclusion: Kochen-Specker contextuality is frame-dependent for relativistic spin systems, with experimentally testable consequences using photon polarisation and a retardation plate.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper investigates whether Kochen-Specker (KS) contextuality is invariant under Lorentz boosts. On the full Hilbert space, boosts are unitary and thus preserve operator identities and contextuality. However, when one restricts attention to the spin degree of freedom, tracing out momentum induces a momentum-dependent Wigner rotation that acts as a quantum channel, making spin observables unsharp and breaking the operator identities that underpin state-independent contextuality. The authors quantify this degradation using a scalar Δ, the packet average of sin²(θ_W/2), where θ_W is the Wigner angle. For spin-1/2, Δ fully characterizes the loss; for higher spin, the degradation rate depends on the spin variance transverse to the boost. The paper then applies this framework to several well-known contextuality and nonlocality proofs: the Free Will Theorem's SPIN axiom, the Yu-Oh set, the Peres-Mermin square, singlet CHSH, and a GHZ-state OR gate. They find that each proof fails at a specific threshold value of Δ: the SPIN axiom fails for any Δ>0; the Yu-Oh set loses contextuality between Δ≈0.008 and 0.016 (state independence first); the Peres-Mermin square loses contextuality at Δ≈0.059 or 0.074 depending on orientation; singlet CHSH loses nonlocality for Δ≥0.159; and the GHZ OR gate loses Raussendorf's contextuality certificate at Δ≈0.206. Finally, they propose that a q-plate can implement the same channel exactly on photon polarization, with a retardation parameter replacing the rapidity, making the nonlocality, GHZ, and aimed-source results testable without actual motion.

title: Graph Neural Post-selection For Quantum Error Correction
authors: Conor Carty, Tamas Noszko, Joschka Roffe, Roberto Bondesan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-selection improves the logical reliability of quantum computation by rejecting shots which are likely to result in logical failure. We introduce graph neural networks that predict decoder failure without additional decoder executions, using only syndromes, and for high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, existing belief-propagation posteriors. We evaluate rotated surface and bivariate bicycle (BB) code memories under uniform depolarising circuit-level noise. Retaining 90% of shots gives approximately 3700x and 740x reductions in logical error rates for [[72,12,6]] and [[144,12,12]] BB codes at realistic physical error rates. For the distance 5 surface code at physical noise p=0.003, our neural post-selector achieves logical error suppression comparable to the leading complementary gap method without running the decoder.
tldr: Graph neural networks post-select quantum error correction shots by predicting decoder failure from syndromes, reducing logical error rates without extra decoding.
motivation: Post-selection can improve logical reliability by discarding likely failures, but existing methods require decoder executions; this work aims to predict failure directly from syndromes.
method: Train graph neural networks on syndrome data, optionally using belief-propagation posteriors for qLDPC codes, to classify shots likely to fail; evaluated on rotated surface and bivariate bicycle code memories under depolarising circuit-level noise.
result: Retaining 90% of shots yields approximately 3700x and 740x logical error rate reductions for [[72,12,6]] and [[144,12,12]] BB codes, and for distance-5 surface code at p=0.003 achieves suppression comparable to the complementary gap method without decoding.
conclusion: Neural post-selection can effectively filter failures in QEC, offering a decoder-free approach that may enhance logical reliability for high-rate qLDPC and surface codes.

title: Symmetry Discovery In Quantum Learning: Observable-Level And Task-Level Inference From Finite Measurements
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00157v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symmetry reduces the capacity of a quantum learning model, but the imposed group must match both the measured information and the label transformation. We establish a finite-measurement theory for inferring this group from candidate transformations. The central structural result identifies observable-invisible transformations with the stabilizer of a projected state whenever the probe span is invariant. It turns recovered generators into a valid subgroup and identifies the continuous invisible space with its Lie algebra. For finite dictionaries, an unbiased shadow statistic distinguishes zero from positive squared expectation discrepancies with an inverse-gap measurement rate, improving the inverse-square-gap rate of uniform discrepancy estimation. A commuting qubit lower bound proves the gap dependence optimal at fixed snapshot scale, and simultaneous intervals support data-dependent tolerances. Task validation then tests either the joint distribution through a characteristic kernel or its encoded mean through a classical--quantum discrepancy. An exact group-average identity relates the latter to joint-state asymmetry and specifies its conversion to binary task breaking mass. Projection bias quantifies the cost of excessive symmetry, while an [MATH] readout bound quantifies the capacity gained by relaxing it. At an invariant pure-state backbone, retained and nontrivial breaking sectors are Fisher-orthogonal. Ising-chain calculations connect finite-shot recovery, label-dependent symmetry, and physical sector drift. These results determine which symmetry the measurements support and provide the statistical and geometric basis for a subsequent release decision.

title: Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes From Lossless Cubical Complexes
authors: Itay Cohen, Itai Leigh, Assaf Reiner, Amnon Ta-Shma, Elad Tzalik
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sipser and Spielman constructed LDPC codes from either bipartite expanders or one-sided expanders. In higher dimensions, expansion similarly played a central role in the constructions of asymptotically good classical LTCs and qLDPC codes by Dinur, Evra, Livne, Lubotzky, and Mozes and by Panteleev and Kalachev. Alternatively, Lin and Hsieh constructed classical LTCs and qLDPC codes from two-dimensional cubical complexes. In this work we develop the higher-dimensional approach. We do not construct the required high-dimensional lossless cubical complexes; rather, we investigate what their existence would imply. We associate with a high-dimensional cubical complex a , whose chain groups are supported on the level sets of the Boolean cube rather than on its cells. Our main technical contribution is a clean local-to-global theorem for this structure: suitable one-dimensional lossless expansion in the directional graphs implies small-set coboundary expansion of the global level complex. As a consequence, sufficiently imbalanced, two-sided lossless four-dimensional cubical complexes give rise to asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes. We expect the local-to-global principle developed here to have further applications.

motivation: Quantum LTCs and qLDPC codes are important for robust quantum error correction, and higher-dimensional lossless cubical complexes offer a promising route beyond existing expander-based and two-dimensional constructions.
method: The authors introduce a level complex supported on level sets of the Boolean cube and prove a local-to-global theorem: one-dimensional lossless expansion in directional graphs implies small-set coboundary expansion of the global level complex.
result: They show that sufficiently imbalanced, two-sided lossless four-dimensional cubical complexes would yield asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes.

title: Characterizing Unitaries Via Quasi-process Functions
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is well-known that every n-qubit unitary can be decomposed into a product of controlled single-qubit unitaries. We show that the control conditions in such a decomposition naturally define a quasi-process function, an object that originally came up in the study of indefinite causal order. Here quasi-process functions yield a representation of every n-qubit unitary in a canonical form, namely, as a quasi-process function unitary (qPFU). We use this representation to show how quantum nonlocality without entanglement (QNLWE) can be understood in terms of unitaries that encode the trade-off between causal order and locality noted in R. Kunjwal and \"A. Baumeler, arXiv:2202.00440. Specifically, we obtain two sufficient (but not necessary) criteria---mutual exclusivity of control conditions (MECC) and Unambiguity---for a unitary to be a process function unitary (PFU), i.e., it admits a qPFU representation where the quasi-process function is a process function, an object that can model paradox-free classical causal loops. We also show the inequivalence of these criteria, neither implying the other. We then show that the circuit depth of MECC unitaries admits a characterization in terms of clique-partitioning problems on Hamming graphs and use this correspondence to provide bounds on the circuit depth of n-qubit MECC unitaries. Finally, we show how MECC unitaries provide a recipe for constructing a unitary purification of the associated process function, thereby providing a large class of unitary processes of interest in quantum causality. The generality of this causality-inspired representation of unitaries makes it a versatile tool for analyzing the structure of quantum circuits in other domains.

result: They obtain two sufficient but inequivalent criteria for process function unitaries, derive circuit depth bounds for n-qubit MECC unitaries via Hamming graph clique partitioning, and provide a recipe for constructing unitary purifications of process functions.
conclusion: The causality-inspired qPFU representation offers a versatile tool for analyzing the structure of quantum circuits and provides a large class of unitary processes relevant to quantum causality and nonlocality without entanglement.

title: Minimax Quantum State Tomography With Periodic Clifford Measurements
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum state tomography provides a foundation for characterizing state preparation and predicting measurement outcomes. We characterize the minimax expected trace norm risk of quantum state tomography over classes with polynomial spectral decay under randomized nonadaptive single copy measurements. Under an explicit sufficient block size condition for the two layer periodic Clifford ensemble, we establish statewise expected trace norm oracle inequalities for operator norm minimum distance and measurement weighted projected least squares, with bounds that depend on each state's actual spectral tail, while the estimators require no prior knowledge of the state's structural characteristics, including its rank, eigenbasis, or spectral structure. Over these polynomial spectral decay classes, both estimators attain the minimax expected trace norm rates up to constants. As a direct consequence, the same estimators attain the minimax rate over every fixed rank constrained class, while remaining adaptive to the unknown structural characteristics of the state. For admissible logarithmic block sizes, the periodic Clifford measurements attain these guarantees with logarithmic elementary gate depth. The main technical ingredient is a uniform bound on the fourth moment of projectors for the periodic Clifford ensemble. The bound is sharp in dimension and holds for arbitrary test states, including those entangled across blocks. Covariance concentration and positivity yield adaptive oracle bounds, while a shared rotation information argument on spectral tail packings establishes matching lower bounds. We also provide polynomial time reconstruction algorithms, numerical comparisons, and Lean formalizations of all labeled theoretical results.
tldr: This paper establishes minimax expected trace norm rates for quantum state tomography using periodic Clifford measurements, with adaptive estimators and efficient reconstruction algorithms.
motivation: Quantum state tomography is fundamental for characterizing quantum states, but optimal measurement design and sample complexity bounds are challenging, especially for states with unknown structure.
method: The authors analyze randomized nonadaptive single-copy measurements from a two-layer periodic Clifford ensemble, prove a sharp fourth-moment bound for projectors, and derive oracle inequalities for operator norm minimum distance and measurement-weighted projected least squares estimators.
result: They show both estimators attain minimax expected trace norm rates up to constants for polynomial spectral decay classes and fixed-rank classes, with logarithmic gate depth for admissible block sizes, and provide polynomial-time algorithms and Lean formalizations.
conclusion: The periodic Clifford ensemble enables adaptive, structure-agnostic tomography with near-optimal sample complexity and efficient implementation.

title: Polynomial-time Local-unitary Equivalence Of Graph States
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local-unitary (LU) equivalence asks whether two quantum states differ only by independent changes of basis on their qubits. For graph states, whether this relation can be decided in polynomial time has remained open for over a decade. We give a deterministic algorithm that decides LU equivalence for graphs on [MATH] labelled vertices in [MATH] bit operations and constructs exact single-qubit unitaries whenever the states are equivalent. Building on Claudet and Perdrix's quasipolynomial algorithm, we replace the enumeration of vertex subsets by a compact system of constraints generated from pairs and triples. The remaining graph transformation is found by solving linear equations over the binary field. These new steps cost [MATH] bit operations; the inherited graph preprocessing sets the overall bound. We also count the local-Clifford (LC) classes of graph states within any LU class: their number is a power of two, computable within the same bound. For any given graph state, this decides whether single-qubit Clifford gates reach every graph state in its LU class, and supplies a counterexample when they do not. The method also decides LU equivalence of stabilizer codes encoding one logical qubit.
tldr: A deterministic polynomial-time algorithm decides local-unitary equivalence of graph states and counts local-Clifford classes within each LU class.
motivation: LU equivalence of graph states has been open for over a decade; deciding it efficiently is important for entanglement classification and stabilizer-code equivalence.
method: Builds on the Claudet-Perdrix quasipolynomial algorithm, replacing vertex-subset enumeration with a compact system of constraints generated from pairs and triples, then solving linear equations over the binary field.
result: The algorithm decides LU equivalence for labelled graph states in polynomial time, constructs exact single-qubit unitaries, counts LC classes within an LU class as a power of two, and decides LU equivalence of stabilizer codes encoding one logical qubit.
conclusion: It provides an efficient solution to a long-standing problem in quantum information, clarifying when single-qubit Clifford gates reach every graph state in an LU class and extending the result to stabilizer codes.

LU equivalence asks whether two n-qubit graph states are related by independent single-qubit unitaries. The authors present a deterministic algorithm that runs in O~(n^{6.38}) bit operations, improving upon the previous quasipolynomial-time algorithm by Claudet and Perdrix. The key innovation is replacing the enumeration of vertex subsets with a compact system of constraints derived from pairs and triples of vertices, and then solving linear equations over the binary field to find the required graph transformation. The new steps cost O~(n^5) bit operations, with the overall complexity dominated by inherited graph preprocessing. The algorithm also constructs the exact single-qubit unitaries when the states are equivalent.

Beyond the main equivalence problem, the paper provides a method to count the number of local-Clifford (LC) classes within any LU class of graph states. The number is always a power of two and can be computed within the same complexity bound. This allows one to decide whether single-qubit Clifford gates can reach every graph state in a given LU class, and to produce a counterexample when they cannot. Additionally, the method extends to deciding LU equivalence of stabilizer codes that encode one logical qubit.

The work builds on the graph-theoretic characterization of LU equivalence, which involves local complementation operations. By formulating the problem as a constraint satisfaction problem over GF(2) and leveraging efficient linear algebra, the authors achieve a significant speedup. The algorithm is deterministic and exact, providing a constructive solution. This result has implications for quantum circuit synthesis, error correction, and the classification of entangled states.

title: Active-Matter Battery
authors: Yun-Qian Lin, Rui-Han Liu, Yu-Han Ma
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Harnessing active matter to power functional devices has attracted growing interest. We propose a minimal battery model for storing energy extracted from active matter and derive its charging and discharging characteristics analytically. When the energetic cost of sustaining activity is included, the charging power-efficiency trade-off becomes loop-like and the efficiency attains a finite-time maximum, in sharp contrast to passive energy devices.
tldr: The paper proposes a minimal battery model that stores energy extracted from active matter and analytically derives its charging/discharging properties, revealing a loop-like power-efficiency trade-off.
motivation: Harnessing active matter to power functional devices has attracted growing interest, but a minimal thermodynamic model for energy storage from active matter was lacking.
method: The authors construct a minimal battery model and analytically derive its charging and discharging characteristics, including the energetic cost of sustaining activity.
result: When the activity cost is included, the charging power-efficiency trade-off becomes loop-like and the efficiency attains a finite-time maximum, contrasting with passive energy devices.
conclusion: Active matter can serve as an energy source for batteries with distinctive finite-time thermodynamic behavior, offering insights for non-equilibrium energy storage.

This contrasts with passive energy devices, where the trade-off is typically monotonic. The work provides a theoretical framework for understanding energy storage in active systems and highlights the role of dissipation in optimizing performance.

title: Exact Replica-sector Hierarchy Of Multi-resolvent Correlations In Random Free Fermions
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The spectral weight with which a many-body eigenstate contributes to a given channel is not fixed by the smooth one-point ETH envelope, and its higher-order correlations---the connected cumulants of three and more channel-resolved spectral functions---have lacked a systematic organization. We construct one. In random free fermions, where every channel overlap is a squared Slater minor of a Haar-orthogonal one-body eigenvector matrix, the [MATH]-resolvent moment admits an exact replica-sector decomposition: a sum over the double-coset sectors of the orthogonal Weingarten algebra, in which the permutation sectors are the replica contraction classes and each sector value is determined by the overlap pattern of the channels and of the eigenstates. The sector coefficients follow from an exact occupancy-matrix assembly---a signed convolution over the slot permutations, a decomposition into connected blocks, and a finite-state chain transfer matrix whose local transition rules are independent of [MATH] and [MATH]---so the sector theorem holds at arbitrary finite multiplicity, realized exactly at [MATH] ([MATH]), [MATH] and [MATH] ([MATH]). The structure carries the physical hierarchy: the fully coincident sector is the projection that yields the Selberg moment ratios [MATH], the levels are nested by exact marginalization, and the sectors are the multi-energy spectral cumulants behind the resolvent cumulants, with the irreducible self-energy vertices of the Feshbach ladder as the connected kernel. The multi-resolvent correlations of random free fermions are therefore organized, level by level, by one replica-sector algebra---an exact microscopic benchmark for the higher-order fluctuation sector of eigenstate thermalization, with its microscopic sector geometry made explicit.
tldr: The paper constructs an exact replica-sector hierarchy for multi-resolvent correlations in random free fermions, organizing higher-order spectral cumulants relevant to eigenstate thermalization.
motivation: Higher-order correlations of channel-resolved spectral functions beyond the smooth one-point ETH envelope have lacked a systematic organizational principle.
method: Using Haar-orthogonal one-body eigenvector matrices, resolvent moments are decomposed into double-coset sectors of the orthogonal Weingarten calculus.

They construct an exact replica-sector decomposition for the r-resolvent moment, expressing it as a sum over double-coset sectors of the orthogonal Weingarten algebra. In this decomposition, permutation sectors correspond to replica contraction classes, and each sector's value is determined by the overlap pattern of channels and eigenstates. The sector coefficients are computed via an exact occupancy-matrix assembly, which involves a signed convolution over slot permutations, decomposition into connected blocks, and a finite-state chain transfer matrix with local transition rules independent of r and k. The sector theorem is shown to hold at arbitrary finite multiplicity, with explicit realizations at r=3 (k=2,3,4), r=4 and r=5 (k=2). The structure reveals a physical hierarchy: the fully coincident sector yields the Selberg moment ratios q_r, levels are nested by exact marginalization, and sectors correspond to multi-energy spectral cumulants behind resolvent cumulants, with irreducible self-energy vertices of the Feshbach ladder as the connected kernel. title: Unifying And Extending Strong Simulation Of Quantum Circuits
authors: Floris Geerts, Rihan Hai, Matthias Lanzinger, Reinhard Pichler, Emanuel Sallinger, Daniel Unterberger
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00547v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish functional aggregate queries (FAQs) as a unifying language for exact classical simulation of quantum circuits. A circuit becomes a sum-product query: factors encode gates, internal wire variables are aggregated, and free boundary variables index transition amplitudes. The central insight is that distinct sources of simulation tractability can be exploited within the same InsideOut evaluation scheme. The query specifies what is computed; the evaluation plan, semiring, and representation of intermediate factors determine the cost. This view unifies structural and algebraic simulation guarantees. With explicit factor representations, FAQ evaluation recovers the treewidth bound for tensor-network contraction and yields finer sparsity-sensitive bounds via fractional covers. Over a formal phase semiring, compressed intermediate factors recover rank-width-based simulation for compatible quadratic phase representations. For Clifford circuits, affine-quadratic factors are closed under multiplication and marginalization and remain polynomial in size, yielding polynomial-time exact amplitude computation without any bounded-width assumption. Beyond these recoveries, the framework yields a new tractability criterion: tensor layout symmetry width. This parameter combines local cut-rank with separator symmetry through exact tree-tensor representations. We give a constructive evaluation bound and exhibit a circuit family with bounded tensor layout symmetry width but unbounded phase-graph rank-width and circuit line-graph treewidth. These results establish representation-aware FAQ evaluation as a common algorithmic foundation for classical simulation and a systematic route to new tractable regimes.
tldr: The paper presents functional aggregate queries (FAQs) as a unifying framework for exact classical simulation of quantum circuits, subsuming and extending existing tractability results.
motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits is central to understanding quantum advantage, but current tractability guarantees are fragmented across different width parameters and algebraic representations.
method: The authors encode quantum circuits as sum-product queries over a semiring and evaluate them via an InsideOut scheme with explicit factor representations, analyzing new parameters such as tensor layout symmetry width.
result: The framework recovers treewidth bounds for tensor-network contraction, rank-width-based simulation for quadratic phase representations, and polynomial-time exact amplitude computation for Clifford circuits, while introducing a new tractability criterion more general than phase-graph rank-width and circuit line-graph treewidth.
conclusion: Representation-aware FAQ evaluation offers a common algorithmic foundation for classical simulation of quantum circuits and a systematic route to new tractable regimes.

title: A Polynomial-time Classical Sampler For Noisy Quantum Circuits From Statistical Mechanics
authors: Jon Nelson, Joel Rajakumar, Chao Yin, Yifan F. Zhang, Michael J. Gullans
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Developing classical simulation algorithms for noisy quantum circuits is essential to delineating the limits of quantum advantage. Existing classical sampling approaches for general circuits require circuit depths to grow logarithmically with system size, so that noise drives the global output state close to a trivial state. Here we show that local accumulation of noise at a depth independent of system size is already sufficient. Specifically, we prove that any geometrically local circuit composed of unital operations and interspersed with single-qubit depolarizing noise of strength [MATH] after [MATH] depth can be approximately sampled from a polynomial-time classical computer. Our proof maps the output state of the circuit to a polymer model in statistical mechanics, and combines a convergent cluster expansion with hypercontractivity of the depolarizing channel.
tldr: Proves that geometrically local circuits with single-qubit depolarizing noise at constant depth can be classically sampled in polynomial time by mapping to a statistical mechanics polymer model.
motivation: Classical simulation of noisy quantum circuits is crucial for understanding the limits of quantum advantage, but existing methods require circuit depths growing logarithmically with system size.
method: Maps the output state to a polymer model and combines a convergent cluster expansion with hypercontractivity of the depolarizing channel.
result: Shows that noise accumulating locally at depth independent of system size suffices for efficient classical approximate sampling.
conclusion: Provides a new depth-independent criterion for classical simulability, tightening the boundary between quantum and classical computation.

title: Nonlinear Collective-spin Dynamics For Quantum-enhanced Sensing In Solid-state Platforms
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Collective spin systems in solid-state materials are promising platforms for quantum-enhanced sensing. In systems such as nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, donor spins in silicon, and magnetic materials, interactions among many spins can generate collective quantum correlations that improve measurement precision beyond the standard quantum limit. This tutorial develops an intuitive, materials-oriented framework for understanding these effects through nonlinear collective-spin dynamics. We show how nonlinear interactions reshape collective spin states in phase space, redistribute quantum fluctuations, and generate metrologically useful states such as spin-squeezed and entangled states. We then connect these ideal collective dynamics to microscopic interactions and realistic solid-state systems, discussing how interaction strength, disorder, decoherence, and experimental control affect sensing performance. Different platforms and experiments are compared to highlight key material properties, advantages, and limitations. The tutorial focuses on a materials-oriented understanding of nonlinear collective-spin sensing, rather than a comprehensive comparison of experimental platforms or a practical guide to sensing experiments.
tldr: This tutorial reviews nonlinear collective-spin dynamics in solid-state platforms for quantum-enhanced sensing, emphasizing spin squeezing and entanglement generation under realistic material constraints.
motivation: Collective spin systems in NV centers, donor spins in silicon, and magnetic materials can surpass the standard quantum limit for sensing via quantum correlations, but an intuitive materials-oriented understanding is needed.
method: It develops a phase-space framework for nonlinear collective-spin dynamics, linking ideal squeezing/entanglement to microscopic interactions, disorder, decoherence, and experimental control, and compares platforms.
result: The tutorial shows how nonlinear interactions reshape collective spin states, redistribute fluctuations, and generate metrologically useful squeezed/entangled states, while material properties and decoherence affect performance.
conclusion: It provides a materials-oriented perspective on nonlinear collective-spin sensing rather than a comprehensive experimental comparison or practical guide.

title: Walshness: An Intrinsic Neural-network Representability Metric For Quantum States
authors: Nisarga Paul, Kehuang Chen, Jessica K. Jiang, Haimeng Zhao, Di Luo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00505v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural quantum states (NQS) have emerged as powerful representations of quantum states with rapidly expanding applications across quantum many-body physics. Yet our understanding of when neural networks can efficiently represent physical quantum states remains limited, in part due to the nonlinear parameterization of NQS, the intricate sign structure of quantum states, and the sensitive dependence on basis choice. We introduce Walshness, a complexity metric of a quantum state which quantifies whether it admits a compact neural-network representation. We rigorously prove that a general quantum many-body state admits an efficient NQS representation if and only if it has bounded Walshness for various NQS architectures. We provide an algorithm for finding the optimal basis by minimizing the energy of a corresponding classical spin model. This allows us to empirically improve the learnability of various physical quantum states, including ground states of the transverse-field Ising model and mixed-field toric code, often reducing infidelity by orders of magnitude, and recovers and generalizes the basis choice given by the well-known Marshall sign rule in frustrated antiferromagnets. Our results provide an intrinsic complexity metric for quantum states with provable connections to their neural-network representability.
tldr: The paper introduces Walshness, a complexity metric that characterizes whether a quantum many-body state admits an efficient neural quantum state representation, and provides an algorithm to optimize the basis for improved learnability.
motivation: Neural quantum states are powerful but their representational efficiency for physical quantum states remains poorly understood due to nonlinear parameterization, sign structure, and basis dependence.
method: The authors define Walshness and rigorously prove that efficient NQS representability is equivalent to bounded Walshness for various architectures; they also develop an algorithm to find the optimal basis by minimizing the energy of a classical spin model.
result: The basis optimization empirically improves learnability of ground states of the transverse-field Ising model and mixed-field toric code, often reducing infidelity by orders of magnitude, and recovers and generalizes the Marshall sign rule.
conclusion: Walshness provides an intrinsic complexity metric for quantum states with provable connections to neural-network representability, offering a practical tool for basis selection and sign-structure exploitation.

title: Noisy Quantum Query Complexity Via Fractional Block Sensitivity
authors: Mehil Agarwal, Shravas Rao, Fang Song
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study quantum query complexity under several models of imperfect oracle access, and develop lower bounds through a common framework based on fractional block sensitivity (\(\fbs\)). For a negligent oracle that applies the correct query with probability \(1-p\), we prove a lower bound in terms of \(\fbs(f,0^n)\). We also show, perhaps surprisingly, that negligence need not destroy quantum speedups: any function \(f\) can be transformed into a partial function \(f'\) whose negligent query complexity essentially preserves the quantum query complexity of \(f\). This gives partial functions with exponential quantum speedups even under negligent queries, and in particular rules out a general lower bound in terms of \(\fbs(f)\) for partial functions in this model. For two other models, we obtain general lower bounds in terms of \(\fbs(f)\) for all Boolean functions. For hybrid algorithms using \(Q\) coherent and \(C\) classical queries, we prove the tradeoff \(C+Q^2=\Omega(\fbs(f))\). For an IID dephasing noisy model where each query dephases the query-index register at rate \(p\) independently, we prove \(\Omega\!\left(p\,\fbs(f)\right)\) queries are necessary. Finally, we introduce a broader family of time-varying dephasing models and identify a variational resource that is always lower bounded by \(\fbs(f)\). Computing this resource reduces to a convex optimization problem, providing a simple way to derive lower bounds for new noise schedules. As applications, we recover the hybrid and IID dephasing bounds and determine the query complexity of unstructured search when the dephasing rate grows over time.
tldr: This paper studies quantum query complexity under noisy oracle models and develops lower bounds via fractional block sensitivity.
motivation: Imperfect oracle access is common in practical settings, but lower bounds for quantum query complexity under noise are less understood than in the noiseless case.
method: The authors use fractional block sensitivity as a unifying framework to prove lower bounds for negligent queries, hybrid classical/quantum queries, and IID dephasing noise, and introduce time-varying dephasing models reducible to convex optimization.
result: They obtain lower bounds in terms of fractional block sensitivity, show negligence does not always destroy exponential quantum speedups for partial functions, and prove a hybrid tradeoff C+Q^2=Omega(fbs) and an Omega(p fbs) bound for IID dephasing.
conclusion: The work provides a general convex-optimization-based resource for deriving query lower bounds under broad noise schedules, with applications to hybrid and dephasing models.

title: Near-Optimal Ground-State Preparation Without Controlled Hamiltonian Evolutions
authors: Dhrumil Patel, Steven T. Flammia, Raul Garcia-Patron
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00520v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ground-state preparation, energy estimation, and property estimation are fundamental tasks in quantum simulation. Existing ground-state preparation algorithms achieve near-optimal complexity using block encodings or controlled Hamiltonian evolution, raising a natural question: is controlled Hamiltonian evolution necessary, or can the same scaling be attained in the weaker access model that provides access to only uncontrolled Hamiltonian evolution? We resolve this question by giving two algorithms that access the input Hamiltonian [MATH] only through queries to [MATH] and its inverse [MATH], where [MATH] and [MATH]. Given an input state with ground-state weight at least [MATH] and a spectral gap of [MATH] of at least [MATH], our first algorithm uses fresh copies of the input state and requires [MATH] queries to [MATH] and [MATH], while our second algorithm uses coherent access to the input-state preparation unitary and its inverse to improve this complexity to [MATH]. The latter bound matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors, showing that algorithms with additional access to controlled Hamiltonian evolution cannot improve the query complexity for ground-state preparation beyond logarithmic factors. Both algorithms are based on a simple mechanism that we call the spectral descent principle, in which the algorithm starts from the input state [MATH] and progressively descends through the energy spectrum, moving closer to the ground state until the desired fidelity is reached. We also extend this framework to ground-state property and energy estimation and give explicit complexity guarantees for both tasks.
tldr: The paper develops near-optimal quantum algorithms for ground-state preparation and energy/property estimation using only uncontrolled Hamiltonian evolution, questioning the necessity of controlled Hamiltonian evolution.
motivation: Ground-state preparation is fundamental in quantum simulation, but existing near-optimal algorithms rely on controlled Hamiltonian evolution or block encodings; this work asks whether the same complexity can be achieved with weaker access to uncontrolled evolution.
method: Two algorithms based on a spectral descent principle are proposed: one uses fresh copies of the input state, and the other uses coherent access to the state-preparation unitary and its inverse, querying the Hamiltonian only through e^{-iHt} and its inverse.
result: The first algorithm achieves a certain query complexity, while the second improves it to match the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors, showing that controlled Hamiltonian evolution cannot improve the query complexity beyond logarithmic factors.
conclusion: The framework is extended to ground-state property and energy estimation with explicit complexity guarantees, demonstrating that near-optimal ground-state preparation is possible without controlled Hamiltonian evolution.

title: Simultaneous Perturbation As A Spectral Filter
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parameterized quantum circuits require repeated measurements to estimate objective gradients, making the number of circuit evaluations a central resource. Simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA) is widely used because it obtains a full gradient estimate from only two cost evaluations, independently of the number of parameters. We analyze the random perturbation for the structured Fourier landscapes generated by quantum circuits. For a finite update width, we derive the exact mode-by-mode response of the mean Rademacher estimator and show that it selectively suppresses modes involving many parameters. For general generators, the filtered mean field need not be conservative. We derive its sampling variance, compare it with Gaussian random-direction smoothing, and formulate the resulting stochastic dynamics through a Fokker--Planck equation. The non-conservative field generates acceleration to the steady state and the global minimum of the cost function by gradually decreasing the parameters in SPSA.
tldr: The paper analyzes simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA) as a spectral filter for gradient estimation in parameterized quantum circuits, revealing how it suppresses certain modes and accelerates optimization.
motivation: Parameterized quantum circuits require repeated measurements to estimate gradients, making circuit evaluations a key resource; SPSA reduces this to two evaluations per step, but its effect on the structured Fourier landscapes of quantum circuits is not well understood.
method: The authors derive the exact mode-by-mode response of the mean Rademacher estimator for finite update width, compute its sampling variance, compare it with Gaussian random-direction smoothing, and formulate the resulting stochastic dynamics via a Fokker-Planck equation.
result: SPSA selectively suppresses modes involving many parameters, the filtered mean field need not be conservative for general generators, and the non-conservative field generates acceleration toward the steady state and the global minimum as parameters are gradually decreased.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical characterization of SPSA's spectral filtering and stochastic dynamics, offering insight into why SPSA can efficiently optimize parameterized quantum circuits.

title: Exact Kernel Transfer To Clique Complexes And The Hardness Of Normalized Persistence

motivation: Normalized persistence is a topological invariant whose computational complexity was not fully understood; the paper aims to establish hardness even under inverse-polynomial spectral gaps and for unweighted complexes.
method: Introduces a finite-certificate kernel-transfer theorem for weighted clique gadgets, simulates a projector Hamiltonian, and encodes a verifier into a fixed eight-dimensional label register; a common-copy blow-up then transfers results to unweighted graphs.
result: Shows additive-error estimation of normalized persistence is hard for the perfect-completeness class over exact gate sets and for finite gate sets with cyclotomic entries, even for unweighted clique complexes.
