title: Quantum Algorithms For Opi Variants Beyond Locality And Classical Decodability
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Regev's reduction is a quantum algorithmic framework for finding codewords satisfying nonlinear constraints by decoding the dual code. To date, applications that have not been dequantized have relied on efficient classical decoders and coordinate-wise constraints specifying a set of allowed values for each coordinate. We push past these two restrictions separately via two separate contributions. Our first contribution uses a quantum decoder to find solutions [MATH] to [MATH], where [MATH]. For fixed prime [MATH], Chen, Liu, and Zhandry (Eurocrypt 2022) solve this problem for random matrices with [MATH], a regime now covered by classical algorithms. We adapt their template to codes (spanned by the rows of [MATH]) with a ``two-fold multiplication property'': the coordinate-wise products of pairs of codewords span a space of dimension much smaller than [MATH]. Our second contribution retains classical decoding but allows global constraints on symbol frequencies. We study ``histogram-local'' constraints, which specify the allowed numbers of occurrences of each symbol. For broad families of these constraints, we show that a uniformly random satisfying vector remains satisfying with constant probability after resampling a uniformly random coordinate. This stability provides sufficient Fourier mass at decodable Hamming weights, yielding efficient quantum algorithms for variants of optimal polynomial intersection (OPI).
tldr: This paper extends Regev's quantum reduction for finding codewords under nonlinear constraints beyond coordinate-wise locality and efficient classical decodability.
motivation: Regev's reduction has enabled quantum algorithms for problems not yet dequantized, but existing applications rely on classical decoders and local constraints, limiting its scope.
method: The authors introduce a quantum decoder for constraints on codewords with a two-fold multiplication property and, separately, allow histogram-local constraints by showing stability under coordinate resampling that yields sufficient Fourier mass at decodable Hamming weights.
result: They obtain efficient quantum algorithms for variants of the optimal polynomial intersection (OPI) problem that go beyond prior locality and classical decodability restrictions.
conclusion: The work broadens the applicability of Regev's reduction in quantum algorithm design for coding-theoretic problems, though it remains algorithmic and not directly connected to quantum information theory topics of interest.

title: Sharp Target-Domain Certificates For Quantum-Kernel Advantage Under Distribution Shift
authors: Roberto Fern\'andez-Barrios, Iker Pastor-L\'opez, Asier Gonz\'alez-Santocildes, Pablo Garc\'ia Bringas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00080v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum predictive advantage under shift usually requires known target labels. We derive the assumption-free sharp identified interval for the finite-batch advantage of a fixed candidate over the best member of a prespecified fixed classical-kernel family under any bounded loss and unrestricted completions of the unaudited labels; zero-one accuracy has exact closed-form partial-label updates. Across eight security shifts, zero-label upper endpoints against 115 classical kernels span 0.002-0.088. Retrospective auditing reduces every endpoint to 0.010 with 0-33 of 500 labels, including entangling-ZZ models. Prospective corroboration on two eligible tasks met predefined criteria: four task-classifier medians require 0-3 labels (overall median 0; maximum 76), and all 20 realized effects are negative; a third task fails its feature gate. Protocol controls reverse an apparent advantage, while finite-shot noise can increase predictive distinctness without useful advantage. The framework separates protocol validity, target predictive indispensability, and quantum relevance.
tldr: The paper derives sharp assumption-free certificates for finite-batch quantum-kernel advantage over classical kernels under distribution shift without requiring target labels.
motivation: Certifying quantum predictive advantage under distribution shift is difficult when target labels are unavailable, motivating assumption-free partial-identification bounds.
method: It computes the sharp identified interval for the advantage of a fixed quantum candidate over a prespecified classical-kernel family under bounded loss and partial labels, with closed-form updates for zero-one accuracy and auditing on security shifts and tasks.
result: Across eight security shifts, zero-label upper endpoints span 0.002-0.088; retrospective auditing reduces all endpoints to 0.010 with 0-33 labels, while prospective tasks meet criteria but realize negative effects and protocol controls reverse an apparent advantage.
conclusion: The framework separates protocol validity, target predictive indispensability, and quantum relevance, showing that apparent quantum-kernel advantage can disappear under proper label auditing and distribution-shift controls.

title: The Kernel-block Rank Profiles Of The $\mathbb{Z}_2\mathbb{Z}_4$-linear And The $\mathbb{Z}_{2^s}$-linear Hadamard Codes, And A Complete Classification Of The $\mathbb{Z}_2\mathbb{Z}_4\mathbb{Z}_8$-linear Hadamard Codes

In this paper, we compute it for the [MATH]-linear and [MATH]-linear Hadamard families with which those codes are compared, and we prove that it is constant for every nonlinear [MATH]-linear Hadamard code and for every nonlinear [MATH]-linear Hadamard code [MATH] with [MATH]. motivation: Hadamard codes over mixed-alphabet rings are difficult to distinguish, and invariants are needed to classify and separate families of such codes.
method: The authors study the kernel-block rank profile, exhibit coordinate permutations that act transitively on kernel blocks, and prove a descent theorem for puncturing on a kernel block.
result: The profile is constant for the nonlinear families considered, separates most nonlinear codes from other linear and nonlinear Hadamard codes of the same length, and leaves only one infinite family that requires a two-block refinement.

title: Spatially Coupled MacKay-Neal Codes On Symmetric Markov Noise: A Reduction To Bms Channels
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a capacity criterion for fixed-degree spatially coupled MacKay--Neal codes on additive symmetric Markov noise. The noise bit flips with probability [MATH], so the channel has one parameter and capacity [MATH]. For every integer [MATH] with [MATH], matched finite-window BCJR and sum-product decoding admit code sequences, possibly depending on [MATH], with actual rate tending to [MATH] and vanishing average information-bit error. The proof parallels the GEC-to-BEC argument: a conditional-entropy correction transfers BMS fixed-point positivity to the channel with memory. The correction also covers a capacity deficit of the effective BMS channel. A two-state posterior contraction supplies the additional derivative bound needed for threshold saturation. The result uses the cited BMS positivity theorem, with an analytic proof for [MATH] and exact interval certificates for [MATH].

motivation: Classical coding theory on channels with memory is important for communication systems, and extending threshold saturation results from memoryless BMS channels to symmetric Markov noise is a natural theoretical challenge.
method: The proof uses a conditional-entropy correction to transfer BMS fixed-point positivity to the Markov channel, along with matched finite-window BCJR and sum-product decoding, and a two-state posterior contraction to obtain a derivative bound for threshold saturation.

title: Hidden-State Updates And Observable-record Composition In Retrocausal Models
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A hidden-variable model can reproduce context-independent individual readouts while failing to preserve observable records when devices are connected or reused. We distinguish two composition requirements. For a finite family of nonnegative instrument matrices, an invariant space generated by normalization defects characterizes unit continuation mass under every finite adaptive policy. Its annihilator defines the maximal admissible positive cone closed under outcome-conditioned updates. A separate observation space characterizes indistinguishability of context-dependent hidden preparations under joint readout. A finite-state example passes every fixed sequence but fails under outcome-dependent stopping. For a wrapped-Cauchy spin source with an explicitly stipulated unchanged-source passive extension, two individually fair probes acquire a setting-dependent agreement probability with contrast [MATH]. More generally, protection under one and two identical uses forces a continuous binary passive response to be constant; measurable two-valued exceptions remain possible. Exact rational calculations, exhaustive finite-policy experiments, continuous source sampling, and quadrature test the stated examples. The criteria apply to specified instrument families and accessible records; they do not construct a microscopic detector or establish consistency under unrestricted network composition.
tldr: Analyzes composition requirements for hidden-variable and retrocausal models, distinguishing invariant spaces for adaptive policies from observation spaces for context-dependent hidden preparations, and shows examples that pass fixed sequences but fail under outcome-dependent stopping.
motivation: To clarify when hidden-variable models preserve observable records under device reuse or connection, beyond merely reproducing context-independent individual readouts.
method: Uses nonnegative instrument matrices, invariant spaces generated by normalization defects, annihilator cones, positive cones closed under outcome-conditioned updates, finite-state examples, a wrapped-Cauchy spin source, exhaustive finite-policy experiments, continuous source sampling, and quadrature.
result: Identifies criteria for unit continuation mass and indistinguishability; a finite-state example fails under outcome-dependent stopping, two individually fair probes acquire a setting-dependent agreement probability, and protection under one or two uses forces a continuous binary passive response to be constant.
conclusion: The criteria apply to specified instrument families and accessible records, but they do not construct a microscopic detector or establish consistency under unrestricted network composition.

title: When Matchgate Base Collapse Fails: A Qutrit Trichotomy And Unbounded Exact Width
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Holographic algorithms solve planar counting problems by encoding each value of a finite domain into several Boolean matchgate wires. Base collapse asks whether every exact representation can be compressed to a number of wires per edge bounded only by the domain size. Chen (STOC 2016) and Xia (STOC 2016) established broad positive collapse theorems under full-rank and related structural hypotheses. Together, these works left open whether a domain-only collapse bound survives when several locally deficient signatures must share one encoding. We resolve this open problem negatively, already on a three-state (qutrit) domain. For every [MATH], we construct a five-label integer-valued qutrit language of maximum arity [MATH] with an exact rational matchgate presentation, yet every exactly equivalent label-preserving presentation requires common width [MATH], even if its domain, base, tensors, and complex weights may all change. The construction avoids the usual local degeneracies, so the obstruction is genuinely simultaneous. Algebraic geometry then drives an exhaustive trichotomy explaining the boundary of collapse: the gadget closure either separates into rays, is Gaussian-mobile and collapses to width at most three, or is confined to a rigid plane-plus-ray flag containing our unbounded family. Pure-spinor geometry forces compression in the mobile case, while dimension bounds for matchgate varieties and Zariski avoidance place exact integer data outside every low-width algebraic image. Thus one geometric framework explains both why collapse occurs and why it can fail without bound.
tldr: The paper disproves a domain-only base-collapse bound for holographic algorithms by constructing a qutrit matchgate language whose exact representations require unbounded common width, and explains the boundary of collapse via algebraic geometry.
motivation: Base collapse theorems (Chen STOC 2016, Xia STOC 2016) guaranteed that exact matchgate representations can be compressed to a width depending only on the finite domain size, but left open whether this survives when locally deficient signatures must share a single encoding.
method: For every arity M the authors construct a five-label, integer-valued qutrit language with an exact rational matchgate presentation that cannot be label-preservingly compressed below width M, then use algebraic geometry (pure-spinor geometry, matchgate variety dimension bounds, Zariski avoidance) to classify gadget closures.
result: The construction avoids local degeneracies and yields a genuine simultaneous obstruction, while an exhaustive trichotomy shows gadget closures either split into rays, are Gaussian-mobile and collapse to width at most three, or fall into a rigid plane-plus-ray flag containing the unbounded family.
conclusion: A single geometric framework accounts for both the success and the unbounded failure of matchgate base collapse, resolving the open problem negatively on a three-state domain.

title: Beyond Lie Algebras: Lie-Wedge Stratification And Pure-State Stabilizability In Single-Channel Qubit Control
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lie algebras describe how control generators combine, but in open systems they erase the distinction between reversible control and irreversible dissipation. Lie wedges retain this information. We study drift-free single-qubit systems with bidirectional Hamiltonian controls and at most one independently actuated dissipator generated by a traceless jump operator. In this work, we prove that they fall into thirteen structural strata defined by the generated algebra and its Lie-wedge geometry. The control algebra and four channel properties determine the stratum; in each wedge, the reversible directions are precisely the coherent controls. We then use the stratification to determine whether a wedge contains a generator with a unique globally attractive pure state. In five strata, stabilizability depends on additional channel data. In one exceptional stratum, no single control-rotated dissipative direction suffices, but averaging two such directions in the wedge yields stabilization. Lie wedges therefore reveal control capabilities that the generated Lie algebra misses.
tldr: The paper introduces Lie-wedge stratification to classify drift-free single-qubit control systems with one dissipator and determine pure-state stabilizability beyond Lie algebra controllability.
motivation: Standard Lie algebra controllability erases the distinction between coherent control and dissipative channels in open quantum systems, motivating a refined geometric tool.
method: The generated algebra and Lie-wedge geometry partition the systems into thirteen structural strata, and channel properties are used to assess whether a wedge contains a generator with a unique globally attractive pure state.
result: Stabilizability is determined in most strata, depends on additional channel data in five strata, and in one exceptional stratum requires averaging two control-rotated dissipative directions for stabilization.
conclusion: Lie wedges reveal control capabilities that the generated Lie algebra misses, providing a finer classification for open-system quantum control.

title: Causal Trade-Offs In Superluminal Extensions Of Relativity. A No-go Theorem
authors: Amrapali Sen, Matthias Salzger, V. Vilasini
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00494v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extensions of relativity that include superluminal reference frames have recently been proposed by Dragan and Ekert as a way to reconcile relativistic symmetry with quantum uncertainty. In this work, we develop a causal modelling framework to formally study this proposal and prove a no-go theorem demonstrating that a theory permitting superluminal reference frames can avoid superluminal signalling only if it severely constrains which spacetime regions are accessible to operational protocols, if the choice of reference frame has observable consequences or if free variables do not exist or their existence depends on the reference frame. Crucially, our result goes beyond the familiar intuition that superluminal transformations may lead to superluminal signalling; our no-go result shows that Dragan and Ekert's proposal of introducing objective uncertainty does not, by itself, eliminate this conflict. In fact, because superluminal signalling might instead be avoided by relaxing other fundamental assumptions in the presence of superluminal reference frames, the proposed objective uncertainty may not be necessary at all. Our results clarify the limitations of uncertainty-based resolutions and the causal trade-offs faced by superluminal extensions of relativity.
tldr: A causal modelling framework is used to prove a no-go theorem showing that superluminal reference frames cannot avoid superluminal signalling without severely constraining spacetime accessibility, frame-dependent observables, or free variables, even with objective uncertainty.
motivation: Dragan and Ekert proposed superluminal reference frames with objective uncertainty to reconcile relativistic symmetry and quantum uncertainty, but it was unclear whether this avoids superluminal signalling.
method: The authors develop a formal causal modelling framework to analyze operational protocols in theories with superluminal reference frames and derive constraints from the absence of superluminal signalling.
result: They prove that any such theory must either restrict accessible spacetime regions for operational protocols, make the choice of reference frame have observable consequences, or deny/relativize the existence of free variables; objective uncertainty alone does not resolve the conflict.
conclusion: The proposed uncertainty-based resolution is insufficient and possibly unnecessary, clarifying fundamental causal trade-offs in superluminal extensions of relativity.

title: First-quantized Quantum Simulation With Non-local Potentials By Matrix-product-state Encoding
authors: Kazuki Tsuoka, Taichi Kosugi, Masari Watanabe, Hirofumi Nishi, Yu-Ichiro Matsushita
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum simulations based on first-quantized approaches can offer lower space and gate complexities than second-quantized approaches. The gate requirements for these simulations can be further reduced by employing pseudopotentials, a technique widely used in classical quantum chemistry calculations to decrease the number of simulated electrons. However, implementing pseudopotentials in quantum circuits remains challenging due to their non-local nature. In this study, we proposed a method to efficiently implement non-local potentials using matrix product state (MPS) encoding. MPS encoding allows us to efficiently implement a Trotter step operator with a circuit depth of [MATH], where [MATH] is the degree of the polynomial local potential, [MATH] is the number of atoms in the system, [MATH] is the maximum number of projector functions across all atoms, and [MATH] is the number of qubits used to represent the binary-encoded wave function in one-dimensional space. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a model of the ionization of a one-dimensional hydrogen atom driven by an ultrashort laser pulse. Our results showed that MPS encoding significantly reduces the required circuit depth compared to a direct unitary decomposition, providing a pathway for practical first-quantized simulations.
tldr: The paper proposes matrix-product-state encoding to efficiently implement non-local pseudopotentials in first-quantized quantum simulation, reducing circuit depth.
motivation: First-quantized quantum simulations can have lower space and gate complexity, and pseudopotentials reduce the number of simulated electrons, but implementing non-local pseudopotentials in quantum circuits remains challenging.
method: The authors encode non-local potentials using matrix product states to implement a Trotter step operator with circuit depth polynomial in the polynomial degree, number of atoms, maximum projector functions, and qubits per 1D wave function.
result: Applied to a model of ionization of a one-dimensional hydrogen atom driven by an ultrashort laser pulse, MPS encoding significantly reduces required circuit depth compared to direct unitary decomposition.
conclusion: The approach provides a practical pathway for first-quantized quantum simulations with non-local potentials.

title: Generative Modeling Of Stochastic Dynamics For Long-Time Evolution
authors: Yang-Yang Tan, Jinyang Li, Lingxiao Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00546v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exact stochastic equations for non-equilibrium dynamics are rarely accessible. We show that the long-time evolution of stochastic dynamics can be predicted from configuration pairs at a fixed short time lag, without knowledge of the equation of motion. Generative diffusion models learn the finite-time transition kernel from these pairs, and iterating it propagates the dynamics far beyond the training lag. For two-dimensional Model B, the diffusive dynamics of a conserved order parameter, the learned kernels reproduce dynamic critical scaling and self-similar [MATH] coarsening. Agreement with direct simulations persists on lattices twice the largest training size and for initial ensembles absent from training. For driven colloids in a periodic optical potential, ten minutes of measured trajectories suffice to predict the particle current and mean passage time over the next twenty minutes within experimental uncertainty. Short-time observations thus contain the information needed to predict emergent non-equilibrium dynamics at much longer times.
tldr: Generative diffusion models learn short-time transition kernels from configuration pairs and iterate them to predict long-time stochastic non-equilibrium dynamics.
motivation: Exact stochastic equations for non-equilibrium dynamics are rarely accessible, so data-driven methods are needed to forecast long-time behavior from limited observations.
method: Diffusion models are trained on configuration pairs separated by a fixed short time lag to learn the finite-time transition kernel, which is then iterated to propagate dynamics far beyond the training lag.
result: The approach reproduces dynamic critical scaling and self-similar coarsening in 2D Model B, generalizes to larger lattices and unseen initial ensembles, and predicts driven colloid currents and mean passage times from ten minutes of experimental trajectories.
conclusion: Short-time observations contain sufficient information to predict emergent long-time non-equilibrium dynamics without knowledge of the underlying equation of motion.

title: Air-llm: Broadcasting Ai Weights Over Radio For Memory-Free Edge Llm Inference Via Rf Computing
authors: Zhihui Gao, Tingjun Chen, Dirk Englund
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00465v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Next-generation large language models (LLMs) are expanding from the cloud to ubiquitous edge devices. However, edge devices typically either lack the memory to store increasingly large LLM weights or, even with enough memory, spend unaffordable energy on loading the weights. This raises our question: can an edge device run an LLM without storing or loading its weights, but receive them over the air and consume them on the fly? Inspired by wireless broadcasting, we present AIR-LLM, an LLM inference architecture for edge devices, which is composed of: (i) a central radio (e.g., 5G base stations) that broadcasts the LLM weights into the air, and (ii) the edge user that receives the weights and completes the general matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV) of LLM inference directly in the radio frequency (RF) domain using RF mixers. To further shorten the airtime, AIR-LLM exploits MIMO spatial multiplexing and proposes an energy-efficient precoder-postcoder pair on the edge to calibrate its own wireless channel. Since the central radio stays user-unaware, AIR-LLM is user-scalable so that one broadcast serves unlimited users within its coverage. We implement AIR-LLM on the NVIDIA Sionna ray-traced channels of two real-world urban scenes and the profiling of a real RF mixer. With a WikiText-2 perplexity degradation of 4.0% on LLaMA-3.1-8B, AIR-LLM saves the energy by 157.7x/40.4x against the FP16 and weight-only quantization baselines; with 20 users, its airtime is 104.1x/26.0x shorter, respectively.
tldr: AIR-LLM proposes broadcasting LLM weights over radio and performing matrix-vector multiplication directly in the RF domain to enable memory-free edge LLM inference with large energy savings.
motivation: Edge devices struggle to store large LLM weights or expend too much energy loading them, motivating an architecture where weights are received over the air and consumed on the fly.
method: The system uses a central radio to broadcast LLM weights and an edge user that computes GEMV in the RF domain with mixers, employing MIMO spatial multiplexing and an energy-efficient precoder-postcoder pair for channel calibration.
result: With 4.0% WikiText-2 perplexity degradation on LLaMA-3.1-8B, AIR-LLM saves 157.7x/40.4x energy versus FP16 and weight-only quantization baselines and shortens airtime by 104.1x/26.0x for 20 users.
conclusion: AIR-LLM demonstrates a scalable, user-unaware broadcast approach for low-energy edge LLM inference, though it is a classical wireless/RF computing contribution rather than a quantum information or thermodynamics result.

title: Quantum Approximate Multi-Objective Optimization In Routing Problems
authors: Eduardo Willwock Lussi, Alisson Dos Passos Fumaco, Marcos Vinicius Reballo, Jos\'e Carlos Libois Neto, Fernando Augusto Caletti de Barros, Eduardo Inacio Duzzioni
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-objective optimization (MOO) problems are common in logistics, where routing decisions must balance conflicting objectives such as travel distance, delivery time, and operational risk. A recently proposed Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) parameter-transfer strategy solves multi-objective MAX-CUT problems by reusing parameters trained on smaller instances, avoiding costly reoptimization for each scalarized problem. However, its effectiveness has only been demonstrated on proof-of-concept instances tailored to quantum hardware connectivity. In this work, we evaluate the applicability of this strategy to realistic routing problems. We formulate the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) and Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) as Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) models, reduce them to MAX-CUT, and assess the parameter-transfer framework under conditions matching the original study. Validation is performed through classical simulations and experiments on IBM quantum hardware. The resulting Pareto fronts are compared with those obtained using an adapted classical {\epsilon}-constraint method, using hypervolume as the primary quality metric. Results indicate that parameter transfer remains effective, frequently achieving higher hypervolume and often finding competitive solutions earlier. However, performance depends on problem structure. The approach is consistently effective for TSP instances but less stable for the more constrained VRP, suggesting that QAOA parameter transferability decreases as the optimization landscape becomes more complex. These results provide the first comprehensive evaluation of QAOA parameter transfer on realistic multi-objective routing problems and demonstrate its potential beyond proof-of-concept MAX-CUT benchmarks.
tldr: The paper evaluates QAOA parameter-transfer strategies for multi-objective routing problems like TSP and VRP via QUBO-to-MAX-CUT reductions, comparing against classical epsilon-constraint methods.
motivation: Multi-objective optimization in logistics requires balancing conflicting objectives, and QAOA parameter transfer could avoid costly reoptimization, but its applicability to realistic routing problems remains untested.
method: The authors formulate TSP and VRP as QUBO models, reduce them to MAX-CUT, and apply a QAOA parameter-transfer framework using classical simulations and IBM quantum hardware, benchmarking hypervolume against an adapted classical epsilon-constraint method.
result: Parameter transfer remains effective for TSP instances, often achieving higher hypervolume and competitive solutions earlier, but is less stable for the more constrained VRP, indicating transferability decreases with landscape complexity.
conclusion: This is the first comprehensive evaluation of QAOA parameter transfer on realistic multi-objective routing problems, demonstrating potential beyond proof-of-concept MAX-CUT benchmarks while highlighting limitations for constrained problems.

title: Entrywise Logarithmic Matrix Algebra And Dichotomy Of Planar Graph Homomorphisms (Part I)
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a complexity classification of counting planar graph homomorphisms with non-negative weights. For a real symmetric matrix [MATH] with non-negative entries, the problem [MATH] is either (1) P-time computable over all graphs, or (2) \#P-hard in general but P-time computable over planar graphs, or (3) \#P-hard over planar graphs. Furthermore, [MATH] in (2) consists of precisely those that involve the P-time FKT algorithm to count planar perfect matchings with a holographic transformation. The dichotomy is achieved by forming a (centered) logarithmic matrix algebra (a vector space with bilinear multiplication) by taking entrywise logarithms of all realizable matrices from [MATH] using planar edge gadgets and polynomial interpolation. The current version is part I, which contains the proof for the dichotomy of entrywise positive and positive definite matrices, which is at the core of the dichotomy for non-negative matrices. Part II contains the extension from entrywise positive and positive definite matrices to non-negative matrices.
tldr: The paper proves a complexity dichotomy for counting planar graph homomorphisms with non-negative weights, using an entrywise logarithmic matrix algebra and the FKT algorithm.
motivation: Classifying the computational complexity of partition functions such as graph homomorphism counts is a central problem in computational complexity, and planar restrictions often lead to unexpected tractability.
method: The authors construct a centered logarithmic matrix algebra by taking entrywise logarithms of matrices realizable from planar edge gadgets via polynomial interpolation; Part I focuses on positive definite and entrywise positive matrices.
result: They establish a trichotomy: the problem is either polynomial-time computable for all graphs, #P-hard in general but polynomial-time for planar graphs via the FKT algorithm, or #P-hard even for planar graphs.
conclusion: This gives a complete complexity classification for non-negative real symmetric matrices in the planar homomorphism problem, with Part II extending the proof to general non-negative matrices.

title: Synthetic Su(3) non-Abelian Gauge Fields In Photonic Synthetic Frequency Dimensions
authors: Bengy Tsz Tsun Wong, Shu Yang, Zehai Pang, Yi Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Synthetic gauge fields provide a powerful route to engineer photonic wave dynamics, especially in synthetic frequency dimensions formed by modulated resonator modes. While most previous realizations have focused on Abelian or lower-rank non-Abelian structures, a photonic implementation of SU(3) gauge fields in the synthetic frequency dimension has remained lacking. Here we propose a route to realize SU(3) gauge structure using three coupled ring resonators with modulation- and interference-engineered mode conversion. We formulate a tight-binding Hamiltonian with matrix-valued hopping generated by the Gell-Mann matrices and show how its evolution can be decomposed into experimentally implementable optical elements. The resulting platform supports SU(3)-structured band dispersions with color-resolved texture and wave-packet dynamics shaped by SU(3) gauge fields. Full-wave-inspired numerical modeling further confirms the expected spectral response and Zitterbewegung-like motion in SU(3) subspaces. Our results introduce SU(3) gauge fields into synthetic frequency photonics and establish a route toward higher-rank non-Abelian control of light in modulated resonator systems.
tldr: The paper proposes an implementation of SU(3) non-Abelian gauge fields in photonic synthetic frequency dimensions using three coupled modulated ring resonators.
motivation: Synthetic gauge fields enable engineered photonic wave dynamics, but prior photonic realizations have been limited to Abelian or lower-rank non-Abelian structures, leaving SU(3) gauge fields unexplored in synthetic frequency dimensions.
method: The authors construct a tight-binding Hamiltonian with matrix-valued hopping generated by the Gell-Mann matrices and decompose its evolution into experimentally realizable optical elements, validating the design with full-wave-inspired numerical modeling.
result: The platform supports SU(3)-structured band dispersions with color-resolved texture, wave-packet dynamics shaped by SU(3) gauge fields, and Zitterbewegung-like motion within SU(3) subspaces.
conclusion: The work introduces SU(3) gauge fields into synthetic frequency photonics, offering a route toward higher-rank non-Abelian control of light in modulated resonator systems.

title: On The Shalit-Shamovich Spectral Radius
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00816v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that the spectral radius introduced by Shalit and Shamovich uniquely determines the underlying operator space structure: If E_1 and E_2 are operator space structures on C^d such that the corresponding spectral radii \rho_{E_1} and \rho_{E_2} agree on every d-tuple of operators, then the identity map is completely isometric. This answers a question of Scherer, Shalit and Shamovich. Moreover, we obtain an analogous result for the minimal spectral radii, and showcase an application to the completely bounded isomorphism problem for algebras of bounded non-commutative functions on operator space unit balls.
tldr: The paper proves that the Shalit-Shamovich spectral radius on operator spaces over C^d uniquely determines the operator space structure up to complete isometry, with an analogue for minimal spectral radii.
motivation: It answers a question of Scherer, Shalit, and Shamovich about whether the spectral radius encodes all operator space data.
method: The author studies spectral radii associated with operator space structures on C^d and compares them on all d-tuples of operators to infer complete isometry.
result: If two operator space structures have the same spectral radius on every d-tuple of operators, then the identity map is completely isometric; a corresponding result holds for minimal spectral radii.
conclusion: The result gives an application to the completely bounded isomorphism problem for algebras of bounded non-commutative functions on operator space unit balls.

title: Closed-form Evaluation Of The Cyclic Four-electron Atomic Correlation Integral
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For positive exponents [MATH] we evaluate the cyclic four-electron Slater integral, the topology recorded as case V in Bonham's 1965 classification, in a finite real expression of weight at most three. The general answer is an explicit sum of eighteen blocks involving only logarithms, dilogarithms and trilogarithms of rational functions of the exponents; all logarithm arguments are positive and all nonconstant polylogarithm arguments may be placed in [MATH], so no radical, generalized polylogarithm, contour prescription or unevaluated limit is required. At equal exponents the value collapses to [MATH], a weight-three period over [MATH] ramified only at 2 and 3. Three independently implemented numerical routes agree at four exponent tuples to at least 32 decimal places, an exact-dyadic evaluation of the classical formula gives eight 100-place certificates, and three published four-electron calibration values are reproduced to every printed digit. We also prove the small- and large-exponent limit laws with closed-form coefficients, dihedral symmetry, and a strict rearrangement law for the three inequivalent cyclic placements of four exponents. The formula applies to the four-cycle and does not evaluate the two chorded topologies.
tldr: Evaluates the cyclic four-electron Slater integral in closed form as a sum of eighteen blocks of logarithms, dilogarithms, and trilogarithms.
motivation: Atomic correlation integrals are needed for accurate electronic structure calculations, but the cyclic four-electron topology lacked a closed-form expression.
method: Using analytic integration techniques, the authors derive an explicit finite expression in terms of polylogarithms of rational functions of the exponents.
result: They obtain a weight-three expression, verify numerically to 32+ decimal places, and prove limit laws and symmetry properties.
conclusion: The formula enables efficient and accurate evaluation of this integral, though it is limited to the four-cycle topology.

title: Self-improvement For Absolutely Ces\'aro Bounded Operators
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that every [MATH]-absolutely Ces\`aro bounded operator with constant [MATH] is [MATH]-absolutely Ces\`aro bounded for [MATH]. This range is optimal, even for positive weighted shifts. On Banach spaces of type [MATH], we prove that every absolutely Ces\`aro bounded operator is [MATH]-absolutely Ces\`aro bounded for every [MATH] for some [MATH]. On [MATH]-spaces, [MATH], we extend the implication from absolute Ces\`aro boundedness to [MATH]-absolute Ces\`aro boundedness from positive to individually eventually positive operators. Finally, for every [MATH], we construct a [MATH]-absolutely Ces\`aro bounded operator [MATH] on [MATH] such that [MATH] but [MATH]. We also observe that the construction yields a single operator which is [MATH]-absolutely Ces\`aro bounded for every [MATH].
tldr: The paper proves self-improvement properties for absolutely Cesàro bounded operators on Banach spaces, including optimal ranges and results on type p spaces and Lp-spaces.
motivation: The work aims to sharpen understanding of absolutely Cesàro bounded operators and their implications for operator ergodic theory on Banach spaces.
method: The author uses functional analytic techniques, including positive weighted shifts as counterexamples, Banach space type conditions, and explicit constructions on Lp spaces.
result: It establishes that α-absolutely Cesàro bounded operators are β-absolutely Cesàro bounded for an optimal range, extends results to Banach spaces of type p and Lp-spaces under individual eventual positivity, and constructs examples showing sharpness.
conclusion: The results advance the theory of absolutely Cesàro bounded operators, but they are unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Full Complexity Dichotomy For Complex-Valued Boolean Holant Problems
authors: Chenghua Liu, Boning Meng, Juqiu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a complexity dichotomy for Boolean Holant problems defined by arbitrary finite sets of algebraic complex-valued signatures. The tractable cases are characterized by an explicit, decidable criterion.
tldr: The paper proves a complexity dichotomy for Boolean Holant problems with complex-valued signatures, characterizing tractable cases via an explicit decidable criterion.
motivation: Holant problems generalize counting constraint satisfaction and are central in classical complexity theory; complex-valued signatures add algebraic and combinatorial complexity.
method: The authors analyze arbitrary finite sets of algebraic complex-valued signatures and derive a decidable criterion that separates tractable from intractable cases.
result: They establish a full complexity dichotomy, proving that every such Holant problem is either tractable or #P-hard, with tractability characterized explicitly.
conclusion: The work resolves the complexity classification for complex-valued Boolean Holant problems, extending prior dichotomies to a broader signature class.

title: A Degree--Size Relation For Resolution Over Polynomials
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For every constant-width CNF, we show that linear degree in polynomial calculus (PC) implies exponential size in resolution over constant-degree polynomials, over the same prime field. Applications include exponential lower bounds for CNFs in [MATH] and hence in [MATH], separations between different moduli, improved lower bounds for [MATH] up to [MATH], proof-search consequences, and an implication of super-polynomial [MATH]-Frege bounds from very strong PC degree lower bounds. The proof uses the common-multiplier idea isolated from Braun [arXiv:2609.23015] to construct a Razborov--Smolensky approximation that preserves inferences, without introducing extension variables. The approximation errors are measured by ranks of the multiplication maps induced by the error-witness polynomials, modulo bounded-degree PC consequences.
tldr: The paper establishes that linear degree in polynomial calculus implies exponential resolution size for constant-width CNFs over constant-degree polynomials, yielding new proof-complexity lower bounds and separations between moduli.
motivation: Understanding trade-offs between degree and size in algebraic proof systems is central to proof complexity, and lower bounds for resolution-style systems have broad consequences for complexity theory and proof search.
method: The proof uses a common-multiplier technique to construct a Razborov–Smolensky approximation that preserves inferences without extension variables, with approximation errors measured by ranks of multiplication maps induced by error-witness polynomials modulo bounded-degree PC consequences.
result: The authors obtain exponential lower bounds for certain CNFs, separations between different moduli, improved lower bounds up to a stated threshold, proof-search consequences, and a derivation of super-polynomial-Frege-type bounds from strong PC degree lower bounds.
conclusion: The work strengthens the connection between algebraic degree lower bounds and resolution size lower bounds, providing a general tool for translating degree constraints into size lower bounds in proof complexity.

title: Complete Factorial Asymptotics And Integrable Structure Of Generalized Charlier Recurrence Coefficients
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the monic recurrence coefficients of the generalized Charlier polynomials associated with the discrete weight \[ \rho_\mu(k) = {(k!)^2}, \qquad k\in\mathbb N_0, \qquad \mu>0. \] We establish complete factorial asymptotics for the deviations [MATH] and [MATH], proving that they are beyond all algebraic orders and appear at the scale [MATH]. The key step is a parametrization [MATH], [MATH], which reduces the problem to a positive sequence [MATH] satisfying a discrete Painlev\'e II equation. Linearization around [MATH] yields a discrete Bessel equation whose recessive solution is [MATH]. We prove that the ratio [MATH] converges to a finite limit [MATH], which we identify exactly as [MATH] by combining Bessel comparison with a global analysis based on the sector decomposition of the associated Hankel determinant. This yields the exact connection formula \[ c_n \sim J_n(2), \qquad n\to\infty, \] and consequently the precise asymptotics \[ \beta_n-n\sim }{n!(n+1)!}, \qquad \mu-\gamma_n\sim }{(n!)^2}. \] We further develop a complementary approach based on Hankel determinants interpreted as a discrete logarithmic gas. We show that the Hankel determinant factorizes as [MATH] and admits a sector decomposition [MATH] with sector contributions independent of [MATH]. We establish [MATH], providing an independent derivation of the factorial corrections. Together, the Bessel comparison and sector decomposition reveal a rich integrable structure linking discrete Painlev\'e dynamics, Toda deformations, and Hankel--partition representations.
tldr: The paper derives complete factorial asymptotics and uncovers an integrable structure for recurrence coefficients of generalized Charlier polynomials.
motivation: Understanding the asymptotic behavior of recurrence coefficients for orthogonal polynomials with discrete weights is a fundamental problem in approximation theory and integrable systems.
method: The authors use a parametrization reducing the problem to a discrete Painlevé II equation, linearize around the limit to obtain a discrete Bessel equation, and independently analyze Hankel determinants via a discrete logarithmic gas and sector decomposition.
result: They prove that the deviations are beyond all algebraic orders, obtain exact connection formula c_n ~ J_n(2), and derive precise factorial asymptotics for beta_n and gamma_n.
conclusion: The work reveals a rich integrable structure linking discrete Painlevé dynamics, Toda deformations, and Hankel-partition representations, with potential applications in random matrix theory and mathematical physics.

title: Intermittent Quarantine Suppresses Epidemic Spreading Beyond Simple Contact Reduction
authors: Silvio C. Ferreira Juliane T. Moraes
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Social interactions are shaped by networks that can be highly heterogeneous, with some individuals potentially interacting with many others. However, physical and temporal constraints limit the number of simultaneous interactions, making social contacts inherently intermittent. Here, we investigate how intermittency affects epidemic spreading on complex networks considering two distinct mechanisms: intermittency of connections (links) and individuals themselves (nodes), with periods of activity and inactivity governed by renewal processes with broadly distributed inter-event times. Combining mechanistic theoretical approaches with stochastic simulations, we show that these two forms of intermittency have fundamentally different effects on epidemic spreading. Link intermittency largely preserves the mechanisms responsible for sustaining transmission, and epidemic behavior can be largely explained by the average reduction in contact opportunities. Contrastingly, node intermittency is substantially more effective at containing spreading because the simultaneous interruption of all contacts suppresses transmission while recovery continues independently. The non-Markovian nature of node intermittency plays a key role: shorter and less heterogeneous inter-event times increase epidemic thresholds and enhance epidemic containment. Our results highlight how the temporal organization of individual activity, beyond the average reduction in contacts, can substantially alter epidemic spreading and may help inform interventions that exploit intermittency in social and biological contact networks.
tldr: Intermittent node quarantine suppresses epidemic spreading more effectively than link intermittency, with non-Markovian temporal organization playing a key role beyond simple contact reduction.
motivation: Social contacts are inherently intermittent due to physical and temporal constraints, and understanding how different forms of intermittency affect epidemic spreading could inform more effective interventions.
method: The authors combine mechanistic theoretical approaches with stochastic simulations on complex networks, modeling link and node intermittency via renewal processes with broadly distributed inter-event times.
result: Link intermittency largely preserves transmission mechanisms and can be explained by average contact reduction, whereas node intermittency strongly increases epidemic thresholds because it interrupts all contacts simultaneously while recovery continues independently.
conclusion: The temporal organization of individual activity, especially non-Markovian node intermittency, substantially alters epidemic spreading and may help design containment strategies in social and biological contact networks.

title: Dilation Theory For Scaled \(q\)-Numerical Ranges
authors: Matias Kaunisto, Ryan O'loughlin, Jani Virtanen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We generalise Berger's dilation theorem from numerical ranges to scaled [MATH]-numerical ranges. Specifically, we prove that if the scaled [MATH]-numerical range [MATH] is contained in the closed unit disk, then [MATH] admits a unitary [MATH]-dilation, where \[ \rho_q=\max\left\{1,{1+}\right\}. \] As a corollary we show that every disk containing [MATH] is a complete [MATH]-spectral set for [MATH]. At [MATH], this recovers the classical fact that any disk containing [MATH] is a complete [MATH]-spectral set for [MATH].
tldr: The paper generalizes Berger's dilation theorem from numerical ranges to scaled q-numerical ranges, proving unitary q-dilations and complete q-spectral set properties.
motivation: It aims to extend classical dilation and spectral set results beyond standard numerical ranges to more general q-deformed numerical ranges.
method: Operator-theoretic techniques from dilation theory and the theory of scaled q-numerical ranges are used.
result: If the scaled q-numerical range is contained in the closed unit disk, the operator admits a unitary q-dilation, and every disk containing it is a complete q-spectral set.
conclusion: The work recovers the classical q=1 case and advances dilation theory for nonstandard numerical ranges, but it is not directly connected to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Interpreting Reasoning Of Large Language Models Via Partial Information Decomposition
authors: Barproda Halder, Qiuyi Zhang, Sanghamitra Dutta
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00571v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved substantial improvements in solving complex mathematical problems, but often produce lengthy, repetitive, or erroneous reasoning trajectories. In this work, we introduce a new interpretability framework, SLIDER, to evaluate the quality of the reasoning process. SLIDER leverages an emerging body of work from information theory called Partial Information Decomposition to disentangle the information about the final answer between two consecutive reasoning steps into non-negative components: unique information (in preceding steps or current step), redundant information, and synergistic information. Building on this decomposition, we propose the *Step-wise Repetitive Reasoning Index (Step-RRI)*, a theoretically grounded measure that assesses whether the answer-relevant information in the current step [MATH] is predominantly redundant with the past steps [MATH], relative to its unique and synergistic contributions. To evaluate the effectiveness of Step-RRI in detecting repetitiveness, we apply SLIDER to the redundancy class of the PRMBench dataset where Step-RRI improves step-level redundancy identification accuracy by over [MATH] points compared to embedding-similarity and information-gain baselines. Next, we define *Trajectory-RRI*, an aggregate measure of repetitiveness for an individual reasoning trajectory. To demonstrate its practical relevance, we show that average Trajectory-RRI strongly correlates with actual reasoning length across QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and GPT-4.1, motivating its use as a signal for improving reasoning efficiency. Finally, we introduce *Trajectory-RRI-guided data selection for fine-tuning*, demonstrating that selecting training data based on Trajectory-RRI can improve a fine-tuned model's reasoning efficiency while largely preserving its task performance.
tldr: The paper introduces SLIDER, a framework using partial information decomposition to quantify redundancy in large language model reasoning steps, with Step-RRI and Trajectory-RRI metrics for detecting repetition and guiding fine-tuning data selection.
motivation: Large reasoning models often produce lengthy, repetitive, or erroneous reasoning trajectories, and there is a need for interpretability tools that assess reasoning quality beyond final answers.
method: SLIDER applies partial information decomposition to disentangle answer-relevant information between consecutive reasoning steps into unique, redundant, and synergistic components, then defines Step-RRI and Trajectory-RRI as measures of redundancy at step and trajectory levels.
result: Step-RRI improves step-level redundancy identification accuracy over embedding-similarity and information-gain baselines, and average Trajectory-RRI correlates strongly with reasoning length across several models; Trajectory-RRI-guided data selection improves fine-tuning efficiency while preserving task performance.
conclusion: The proposed information-theoretic measures provide a theoretically grounded way to detect redundancy in LLM reasoning and can be used to improve reasoning efficiency through data selection and fine-tuning.

title: Fixed-Time Iss For Interconnected Discrete-Time Systems, Part Ii: Finite-Horizon Lyapunov Functions
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study fixed-time input-to-state stability (FxT-ISS) for discrete-time systems subject to exogenous inputs using finite-horizon Lyapunov functions. In the proposed Lyapunov- based characterization, the effect of the initial condition is eliminated after a uniformly bounded number of iterations. This characterization encompasses existing extinction-based Lyapunov conditions while allowing more general finite-memory mechanisms. Building on this framework, we establish a finite-horizon small-gain theorem for interconnected discrete-time systems, providing conditions under which FxT-ISS is preserved under feedback interconnections. The proposed framework is illustrated through examples arising in distributed algorithms, optimization, and feedback optimization.
tldr: The paper develops a finite-horizon Lyapunov characterization of fixed-time input-to-state stability for interconnected discrete-time systems, including a small-gain theorem.
motivation: Fixed-time stability is important for control and optimization algorithms that require convergence within a uniformly bounded time independent of initial conditions.
method: The authors introduce finite-horizon Lyapunov functions where the initial-condition effect vanishes after a bounded number of iterations, and use them to prove a small-gain theorem for feedback interconnections.
result: The framework generalizes extinction-based Lyapunov conditions and provides conditions under which fixed-time ISS is preserved under interconnection, illustrated by distributed algorithms and feedback optimization examples.
conclusion: The proposed finite-horizon Lyapunov approach offers a flexible tool for analyzing fixed-time stability in interconnected discrete-time systems with exogenous inputs.

title: Integration Of External Predictions For Efficient Estimation Of The Risk Ratio
authors: Victoria Mezger, Nils Kr\"uger, Georg Hahn
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the augmentation of randomized experiments or trials with data from observational studies for the purpose of improving statistical precision. In particular, we focus on the Hybrid Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting estimator, designed to integrate predictions from several foundation models while preserving valid statistical inference. In this article, we extend the Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting framework to the estimation of the risk ratio, the quotient of the absolute risk of an exposed to an unexposed group. Our approach allows one to use information from black-box foundation models trained on external and possibly unstructured data, yielding an estimator of the risk ratio whose asymptotic variance is never larger than the one of the default estimator based on experimental data alone.
tldr: The paper extends the Hybrid Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting estimator to estimate the risk ratio, integrating predictions from foundation models trained on external observational data to improve statistical precision in randomized trials.
motivation: Randomized experiments often have limited sample sizes, but external observational data and black-box foundation model predictions could be leveraged to increase statistical precision while preserving valid inference.
method: The authors extend the Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (AIPW) framework, specifically the Hybrid AIPW estimator, to the risk ratio by incorporating predictions from several foundation models while maintaining asymptotic validity.
result: The proposed risk ratio estimator has an asymptotic variance that is never larger than that of the default estimator using experimental data alone.
conclusion: Integrating external model predictions into AIPW-style estimation yields a principled, never-worse estimator of the risk ratio for augmented randomized trials.

title: Uncertainty Quantification For Landweber Iteration With Randomized Normal-Operator Approximation
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00882v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Iterative methods are extremely popular for solving linear ill-posed inverse problems. While deterministic convergence, or more precisely, semi-convergence of such methods is widely studied, the problem of quantifying uncertainty in the resulting reconstructions due to random noise in the observed data has received far less attention. In this work, we study uncertainty quantification for the Landweber iteration in linear inverse problems using the Radon transform as a motivating example. We interpret the Landweber reconstruction statistically by analyzing how uncertainty in the measured data is propagated through the reconstruction map. This perspective is closely related to generalized fiducial inference, where uncertainty about the parameter is induced by inverting the relation between the observed data and the unknown (fixed) quantity. We combine the resulting stochastic uncertainty with a theoretical bound on the regularization bias to construct confidence intervals for the reconstructed solution. The evaluation of the resulting uncertainty estimates require repeated operations with the forward operator that can become expensive in large-scale problems. To reduce this cost, we use randomized singular value decomposition to obtain a low-rank approximation of the normal operator associated with the Radon transform and incorporate this approximation in quantifying uncertainty. {{In particular, this requires that the additional randomization error introduced due to the use of such randomized techniques be included in our approach for uncertainty quantification.}} Numerical results show that the proposed method provides accurate reconstructions and reliable uncertainty estimates at substantially reduced computational cost.
tldr: The paper develops uncertainty quantification for the Landweber iteration applied to linear ill-posed inverse problems, using a randomized low-rank approximation of the normal operator to reduce computational cost.
motivation: While deterministic convergence (semi-convergence) of iterative regularization methods like Landweber is well studied, quantifying the uncertainty of reconstructions due to random noise in observed data has received little attention.
method: The authors interpret the Landweber reconstruction statistically via a generalized fiducial inference perspective, propagate data uncertainty through the reconstruction map, and combine it with a theoretical regularization-bias bound to build confidence intervals; randomized SVD provides a low-rank approximation of the normal operator (with the additional randomization error incorporated).
result: Numerical experiments using the Radon transform show accurate reconstructions and reliable uncertainty estimates at substantially reduced computational cost compared to exact normal-operator operations.
conclusion: The proposed randomized framework yields practical confidence intervals for Landweber reconstructions in large-scale inverse problems, balancing statistical uncertainty with estimation bias.

title: Approximate Polynomial Satisfiability Is In The Counting Hierarchy
authors: Nikhil Balaji, Mahsa Shirmohammadi, S\'ebastien Tavenas, James Worrell
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Approximate polynomial satisfiability problem (APS), introduced by Guo, Saxena, and Sinhababu (CCC 2018), asks whether the zero vector lies in the Zariski closure of the image of a given polynomial map. Specifically, for a field [MATH] with algebraic closure~[MATH], the problem asks whether [MATH] for a polynomial map [MATH] with [MATH]. APS is a natural topological analogue of Hilbert's Nullstellensatz, namely the question of whether a given system of polynomial equations has a common zero. APS captures several problems in algebraic complexity, including border rank, hitting sets for border classes, and null-cone membership; it is known to be NP-hard and in PSPACE. We show that APS lies in the Counting Hierarchy (CH) over both the rationals and finite fields, substantially improving the known PSPACE upper bound. Our proof builds on a recent breakthrough due to Andrews, Garg, and Schost (FOCS 2026) on deciding Hilbert's Nullstellensatz in CH. As a corollary, our result improves the complexity of certifying hitting sets for border classes from PSPACE to CH. We also give a polynomial-time reduction of Hilbert's Nullstellensatz to APS, valid in any characteristic. In characteristic zero, we give a reduction of APS to the decision problem for the existential theory of real closed fields. Overall, our results place approximate polynomial satisfiability closer in complexity to exact polynomial feasibility and as a byproduct give improved complexity bounds for several problems arising in approximative complexity.
tldr: The paper shows that the Approximate Polynomial Satisfiability problem lies in the Counting Hierarchy, improving the previous PSPACE upper bound.
motivation: APS is a natural topological analogue of Hilbert's Nullstellensatz and captures problems in algebraic complexity such as border rank and hitting sets for border classes.
method: The proof builds on a recent breakthrough by Andrews, Garg, and Schost on deciding Hilbert's Nullstellensatz in the Counting Hierarchy, extending it to the approximate setting over rationals and finite fields.
result: APS is placed in CH over both the rationals and finite fields, yielding improved complexity bounds for certifying hitting sets for border classes and other problems in approximative complexity.
conclusion: The results bring approximate polynomial satisfiability closer in complexity to exact polynomial feasibility and provide reductions to Hilbert's Nullstellensatz and the existential theory of real closed fields.

title: Progressive-Resolution Secure Aggregation For Federated Learning
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Secure aggregation lets a server recover an aggregate of client updates without observing any individual update, but conventional protocols fix the aggregate precision when clients upload. We introduce and formulate a new progressive-resolution secure-aggregation functionality in which clients upload once and successively finer resolutions of the same aggregate can later be authorized without renewed client participation. To realize this functionality, we propose progressive-resolution secure aggregation (PSA): each clipped, dithered update is represented by compatible nested-lattice digits; separately releasable layers are protected by secure aggregation and an additional aggregate pad that remains unavailable to the server until a non-colluding release controller authorizes that layer.
tldr: The paper proposes a progressive-resolution secure aggregation protocol for federated learning that allows clients to upload once while enabling successively finer aggregate resolutions to be released later under controlled authorization.
motivation: Conventional secure aggregation fixes aggregate precision at upload time, preventing later access to finer resolutions without renewed client participation.
method: Each clipped and dithered client update is decomposed into compatible nested-lattice digits, with separately releasable layers protected by secure aggregation and an aggregate pad that requires a non-colluding release controller to authorize.
result: The proposed PSA functionality enables progressive-resolution release of aggregate information from a single client upload, maintaining privacy against the server until a layer is authorized.
conclusion: The work introduces a new secure aggregation functionality for federated learning, but it is a classical cryptography and privacy-preserving machine learning contribution with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Reading While Writing: Baseline Information Requirements For Molecular Neural Interfaces
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Molecular neural interfaces that deliver and sense the same neurotransmitter must estimate endogenous release in the presence of their own chemical input. We study two exchanging regions with shared saturable uptake and concentration change measurements. Known delivery and exchange permit identification of apparent uptake at the driven region, but an unknown resting concentration difference leaves the source region's incremental uptake uncertain. We characterize all admissible source histories consistent with both ideal records and show how delivery and baseline information affect release classification. A dopamine-inspired example produces identical ideal concentration-change records for mean release-rate changes of -8.99 and +1.31 nanomolar per second. Stronger delivery changes whether all compatible sources imply suppression, with the true source held fixed. Under a Gaussian observation model, we bound discrimination based on chemical fluctuations. A baseline reference with an assumed standard deviation of 3.3 nanomolar reduces root-mean-square error from 10.41 to 1.21 nanomolar per second compared with an incorrect fixed baseline under exact gain calibration. Classification errors remain substantial with weak excitation, gain errors or responses near the category boundaries.
tldr: The paper analyzes the baseline information needed to correctly classify endogenous neurotransmitter release when a molecular neural interface both delivers and senses the same neurotransmitter.
motivation: Molecular neural interfaces that simultaneously deliver and sense the same neurotransmitter must disentangle their own chemical input from the neuron's endogenous release, which requires understanding what baseline information is necessary for reliable inference.
method: The authors model two exchanging regions with shared saturable uptake and concentration-change measurements, characterize all admissible source histories consistent with ideal records, and use a Gaussian observation model to bound release discrimination from chemical fluctuations.
result: They show that unknown resting concentration differences leave the source region's incremental uptake uncertain, that distinct release-rate changes (-8.99 and +1.31 nM/s) can produce identical ideal records, and that an assumed 3.3 nM baseline reference reduces RMSE from 10.41 to 1.21 nM/s under exact gain calibration.
conclusion: Baseline and delivery information fundamentally limit release classification, with errors remaining substantial under weak excitation, gain errors, or responses near category boundaries.

title: SafeDepth: Safety-Aware Token-Level Adaptive Computation
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent studies suggest that not every token needs to pass through all Transformer layers, motivating token-level adaptive models that selectively skip layers to reduce computation. Our experiments show that these execution choices also affect safety: existing token-level adaptive reasoning models exhibit higher harmful-response rates than their reference backbones. The safety effects depend on which layers are skipped and whether skipping occurs during prompt processing or answer generation. We further find that recognizing harmful requests and producing refusals depend on different layer-wise computations. We introduce SafeDepth, a lightweight, plug-in framework that uses selective layer execution to improve both safety and efficiency. SafeDepth learns to retain computations that support safe responses and bypass those that contribute to unsafe generation. A router selects layer execution based on token representations, layer position, and inference phase, while an adapter supports the skipped paths. We jointly train these modules to reduce computation and harmful responses while preserving performance on benign tasks, targeting a better safety-efficiency trade-off. The pretrained backbone remains frozen throughout, requiring no additional pretraining. Experimental results on Llama-3-8B-Instruct show that SafeDepth reduces computation relative to full-depth inference while largely preserving task performance. Compared with FlexiDepth, it lowers unsafe-response rates across all five harmful-request benchmarks, with the largest absolute decrease on HarmBench-HJ (from 55.44% to 25.25%), while reducing the XSTest false-refusal rate from 12.0% to 4.0%.
tldr: SafeDepth is a plug-in framework for token-level adaptive layer skipping in LLMs that aims to improve both safety and computational efficiency.
motivation: Existing token-level adaptive models can reduce computation but exhibit higher harmful-response rates, and the safety impact depends on which layers are skipped and during which inference phase.
method: SafeDepth uses a router to select layer execution based on token representations, layer position, and inference phase, with an adapter to support skipped paths, jointly trained while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen.
result: On Llama-3-8B-Instruct, SafeDepth reduces computation while largely preserving benign task performance and lowers unsafe-response rates across five harmful-request benchmarks, with the largest drop on HarmBench-HJ from 55.44% to 25.25%, and reduces XSTest false refusals from 12.0% to 4.0%.
conclusion: Selective layer execution can jointly improve safety and efficiency in LLM inference, offering a better safety-efficiency trade-off without additional pretraining.

title: Predictor-Based Exponential Tracking Of Turbulent Solutions For The Kuramoto--Sivashinsky Equation With Input Delay
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Uniform exponential tracking is addressed for nonstationary trajectories of the nonlinear Kuramoto--Sivashinsky equation subject to a constant input delay. The reference belongs to a family of complete trajectories contained in the global attractor and need not be stationary, periodic, slowly varying, or generated by a finite-dimensional exosystem. The delayed input is represented by a first-order transport equation coupled with the fourth-order tracking-error dynamics. A predictor--backstepping transformation compensates for the temporal mismatch between command generation and actuation by mapping the augmented closed-loop system into the nominal delay-free error dynamics driven by the outgoing trace of a homogeneous transport subsystem. This subsystem vanishes after one delay interval. Uniform attractor bounds permit the feedback parameters and stability constants to be selected independently of the initial time and the reference trajectory. Global well-posedness and uniform exponential stability are established in the augmented state space. Numerical results show that, for the considered configuration, uncompensated delayed feedback amplifies the tracking error, whereas predictor compensation restores sustained decay. Predictor-consistency, finite-time-extinction, and discretization-refinement diagnostics support the numerical implementation.
tldr: The paper develops a predictor-based backstepping control law to achieve uniform exponential tracking of turbulent trajectories of the delayed Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation.
motivation: Input delays in nonlinear distributed-parameter systems can destabilize tracking and amplify errors, so compensation is needed for reliable control of nonstationary turbulent dynamics.
method: A first-order transport equation represents the delayed input, and a predictor–backstepping transformation maps the augmented system into nominal delay-free error dynamics whose homogeneous transport subsystem vanishes after one delay interval.
result: Global well-posedness and uniform exponential stability are proved in the augmented state space, with numerical simulations showing that predictor compensation restores sustained decay whereas uncompensated delayed feedback amplifies tracking error.
conclusion: Predictor-based backstepping provides an effective framework for exponential tracking of turbulent Kuramoto–Sivashinsky solutions under constant input delay, with diagnostics supporting numerical implementation.

title: New Pareto Z-eigenvalue Localization Theorems For Tensors With Applications
authors: Licai Shao, Xingong Shao, Yisheng Song
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we establish some new localization sets for Pareto Z-eigenvalues of tensor eigenvalue complementarity problems and discuss the relationships among existing ones. As applications, a sufficient condition for the solution existence of the tensor complementarity problem (TCP) and the tensor generalized eigenvalue complementarity problem (TGEiCP) are presented. In addition, this condition is also used to test the vacuum stability of a general scalar potential.
tldr: The paper establishes new localization sets for Pareto Z-eigenvalues of tensors and applies them to tensor complementarity problems and vacuum stability testing.
motivation: Localization of tensor eigenvalues is important for understanding tensor eigenvalue complementarity problems and for deriving existence conditions.
method: New localization theorems for Pareto Z-eigenvalues are derived, relationships among existing sets are discussed, and applications to tensor complementarity problems and scalar potential vacuum stability are presented.
result: Sufficient conditions for the solution existence of TCP and TGEiCP are obtained, and these conditions are used to test vacuum stability of a general scalar potential.
conclusion: The work advances tensor eigenvalue complementarity theory but is not directly related to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Control Of 1d First-order Linear Hyperbolic Systems: A Brief Survey
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: At the occasion of the 70th birthday anniversary of Jean-Michel Coron, we review the literature on the control of 1D first-order linear hyperbolic systems, a topic where he has made significant contributions.
tldr: A survey reviewing the literature on the control of one-dimensional first-order linear hyperbolic systems, honoring Jean-Michel Coron's contributions.
motivation: Written to mark Jean-Michel Coron's 70th birthday, the survey collects and organizes results in a control-theoretic area where he made foundational contributions.
method: Literature review that synthesizes existing results on controllability, stabilization, and boundary control for 1D first-order linear hyperbolic PDE systems.
result: Provides a structured overview of known theorems and techniques in hyperbolic PDE control rather than presenting new technical results.
conclusion: Serves as a reference survey for the PDE control community, with no direct connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Reachability And Exact Controllability Of Linear Stieltjes Differential Systems
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study reachability and exact controllability for systems driven by a nondecreasing left-continuous Stieltjes derivator whose measure may have continuous, singular-continuous and atomic parts, while flat intervals represent inactivity. We construct an evolution family and post-jump variation-of-constants formula, and characterize the reachable subspace as the essential span of input directions. For constant coefficients, the Kalman condition is necessary for every derivator and, under regressivity, sufficient when the derivator is continuous and nonconstant on a subinterval. If the measure is purely atomic with exactly [MATH] positive atoms, the reachable subspace is the truncated Krylov space generated by [MATH]; for a Kalman-controllable pair, the minimum atom count among purely atomic derivators equals the controllability index. At the threshold count, one vanishing mass with the others converging to positive finite limits causes Gramian degeneration and worst-case energy blow-up; at or above threshold, compact positive mass ranges yield uniform coercivity. A mixed double-integrator example illustrates the results.
tldr: The paper studies reachability and exact controllability for linear systems driven by a nondecreasing left-continuous Stieltjes derivator with continuous, singular-continuous, and atomic measure parts.
motivation: Control theory for differential equations with measure-valued derivatives is less developed, and the authors aim to characterize reachability when the derivative measure may have mixed continuous and atomic components.
method: They construct an evolution family and a post-jump variation-of-constants formula, then characterize the reachable subspace as an essential span of input directions, deriving Kalman-type conditions and connections to Krylov spaces for purely atomic measures.
result: The Kalman condition is necessary for all derivators and sufficient under regressivity and continuity assumptions; for atomic measures the reachable subspace is a truncated Krylov space, and threshold atom counts lead to Gramian degeneration and energy blow-up.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic framework for reachability and exact controllability of linear Stieltjes differential systems, illustrated by a mixed double-integrator example.

title: Sharp High-Probability Statistical Rates For Heavy-Tailed Nonsmooth Convex Optimization
authors: Haihan Zhang, Wendao Wu, Chenheng Zhang, Yanyi Li, Chunyuan Zheng, Cong Fang, Haoxuan Li, Zhouchen Lin
