abstract: ArXiv:2610.00260v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish sharp high-probability statistical rates for nonsmooth stochastic convex optimization under heavy-tailed noise, closing the confidence-dependence gap in both general convex and strongly convex settings. We consider composite objectives with a Lipschitz convex loss and a known proximal regularizer, accessed through fresh unbiased stochastic subgradients. The centered noise has conditional norm and directional [MATH]th moments bounded by [MATH] and [MATH], respectively, where [MATH], set [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH]. With initial distance bound [MATH], the minimax objective error is [MATH] in the nonsaturated statistical regime. For a [MATH]-strongly convex regularizer, the corresponding quadratic-regime rate is [MATH]. These rates require domination of the deterministic and finite-variance terms; matching lower bounds require [MATH], while the upper bounds hold in every finite dimension. The new upper bounds attain known statistical lower-bound orders, replacing the previous confidence coefficient [MATH] by [MATH], and its square by [MATH] under strong convexity. The key is an online inequality that separates directional fluctuations from the total second moment created by rejection sampling. Localization preserves this separation under strong convexity without additional horizon logarithms. The results characterize oracle complexity with unrestricted internal computation.
tldr: The paper derives sharp high-probability statistical rates for nonsmooth stochastic convex optimization under heavy-tailed noise, closing the confidence-dependence gap in both general and strongly convex settings.
motivation: Existing high-probability convergence guarantees for nonsmooth stochastic convex optimization degrade poorly with confidence level, especially under heavy-tailed noise where only bounded moments are assumed.
method: Using fresh unbiased stochastic subgradients with bounded conditional norm and directional high-order moments, the authors prove an online inequality separating directional fluctuations from the total second moment induced by rejection sampling, plus localization arguments for strong convexity.
result: The minimax objective error rate improves from a 1/delta dependence to log(1/delta)/delta dependence, with the square root of this improvement under strong convexity, matching known lower-bound orders in the nonsaturated statistical regime.
conclusion: The work characterizes the oracle complexity of nonsmooth stochastic convex optimization under heavy tails and establishes near-optimal confidence dependence, though the topic lies outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Schwarz-Pick And Denjoy-Wolff For Uniformly Quasiregular Maps
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00312v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a Denjoy-Wolff theorem for uniformly quasiregular self-maps of the unit ball in [MATH], [MATH]: either all orbits are relatively compact, or the iterates converge locally uniformly to a single point of the sphere. No properness, surjectivity, or boundary extension is assumed. The key tool is a Schwarz-Pick lemma valid in all dimensions: every quasiregular map preserving a bounded measurable conformal structure is non-expanding for a modulus metric built from that structure, and uniformly quasiregular maps preserve such a structure by a theorem of Iwaniec and Martin. Since this metric is not geodesic, we pass to an associated chain metric, which we show is Gromov hyperbolic with boundary the sphere, and apply a theorem of Karlsson. As an application, a stable Fatou component of a uniformly quasiregular map of [MATH] that is a uniform domain with uniformly perfect boundary is an attracting basin, a rotation domain, or a parabolic basin with a unique boundary fixed point. Non-injective examples of both escaping types are constructed in every dimension.
tldr: The paper extends Schwarz-Pick and Denjoy-Wolff theorems to uniformly quasiregular self-maps of the unit ball in higher dimensions using a modulus metric and chain metric approach.
motivation: Classical complex dynamics results such as Denjoy-Wolff are well understood in one dimension, and the authors seek generalization to quasiregular maps in all dimensions without properness, surjectivity, or boundary extension assumptions.
method: They prove a Schwarz-Pick lemma for quasiregular maps preserving a bounded measurable conformal structure, pass to an associated chain metric shown to be Gromov hyperbolic with the sphere as boundary, and apply Karlsson's theorem.
result: They obtain a Denjoy-Wolff dichotomy for uniformly quasiregular maps and characterize stable Fatou components as attracting, rotation, or parabolic basins, constructing non-injective examples in every dimension.
conclusion: The work advances quasiconformal dynamics and complex analysis but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Q-mino: A Minimal-Norm Method For Quantization-Aware Training
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00738v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Straight-Through Estimator (STE) is a widely used heuristic for Quantization-Aware Training (QAT), but its surrogate gradients can exhibit substantial mismatch with the underlying quantized objective, leading to noisy updates and parameter oscillations, particularly in ultra-low-bit regimes. We propose the Quantization-Aware Minimal-Norm Optimizer (Q-MINO), a temporal bundle method that combines gradient consensus, state-drift regularization, and an alignment constraint to construct stabilized, minimum-norm update directions from recent optimization states. Q-MINO solves the resulting constrained subproblem using a warm-started Frank--Wolfe procedure with a feasible fallback initialization. Theoretically, via a stochastic Lyapunov Kurdyka--\L ojasiewicz (KL) framework, we show that Q-MINO achieves asymptotic neighborhood convergence. Moreover, we detail numerical experiments with Q-MINO at various quantizations.
tldr: Q-MINO is a minimal-norm optimization method for quantization-aware training that mitigates straight-through estimator gradient mismatch in ultra-low-bit regimes.
motivation: The straight-through estimator used in quantization-aware training produces surrogate gradients that poorly match the true quantized objective, causing noisy updates and parameter oscillations at low bit-widths.
method: The authors propose a temporal bundle method combining gradient consensus, state-drift regularization, and an alignment constraint, solving a constrained minimum-norm subproblem via a warm-started Frank-Wolfe procedure with a feasible fallback initialization, analyzed through a stochastic Lyapunov Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz framework.
result: Q-MINO is shown to achieve asymptotic neighborhood convergence and is evaluated numerically across several quantization settings.
conclusion: The method offers a more stable optimization direction for quantization-aware training, though the work concerns classical deep-learning optimization and has no connection to quantum information or quantum thermodynamics.

title: A Riccati Approach To Mixed $H_2/H_\infty$ Closed-Loop Games For Infinite-Dimensional Stochastic Systems
authors: Mingyang Shen, Weihai Zhang, Qingxin Meng, Maoning Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies a finite-horizon mixed [MATH] feedback Nash game for stochastic evolution equations on a separable Hilbert space. The drift generator is unbounded, the remaining coefficients are bounded, and the one-dimensional Brownian diffusion depends on the state, control, and disturbance. The [MATH] channel is an LQ state--control energy. For the disturbance channel, the stochastic LQ uniform-convexity characterization yields equivalence between strict induced [MATH] attenuation and unique strongly regular mild Riccati solvability. Simultaneous bounded-generator approximation of the Lyapunov equation and the state justifies quadratic identities for strongly continuous mild operator solutions. These identities verify both Nash inequalities and full-output strict attenuation from a strongly regular coupled Riccati pair. An invertible feedback block and a contraction argument establish locally unique coupled solutions on a sufficiently short terminal interval for every positive attenuation level. For a specified stochastic heat-equation model at [MATH], a uniform invariant rectangle further proves full-horizon existence, bounded infinite-dimensional feedbacks, and operator-norm spectral convergence. Numerical computations reproduce the projected gains and compare selected best responses. Global coupled solvability for general coefficients remains an explicit hypothesis.
tldr: The paper develops a Riccati-equation framework for finite-horizon mixed H2/H∞ feedback Nash games governed by stochastic evolution equations on a Hilbert space.
motivation: Mixed H2/H∞ control aims to balance mean-square performance against worst-case disturbance attenuation, but existing treatments for infinite-dimensional stochastic systems with unbounded drift lack a rigorous closed-loop game formulation.
method: Using stochastic LQ uniform-convexity characterizations, bounded-generator approximation of Lyapunov equations, and a contraction/invertible-feedback argument, the authors construct strongly regular mild solutions of coupled Riccati equations.
result: Strict induced-L2 attenuation is shown equivalent to unique strongly regular mild Riccati solvability, yielding Nash inequalities and full-output attenuation; a stochastic heat-equation example gives full-horizon existence and operator-norm spectral convergence.
conclusion: The work extends mixed H2/H∞ game theory to infinite-dimensional stochastic systems with unbounded drift, though global coupled solvability for general coefficients remains an open hypothesis.

title: A Comprehensive Review Of One-Pixel Attack: Research Status, Taxonomy, Applications, Regulation Policy And Future Directions
authors: Mirza Niaz Morshed, Md. Masudul Islam, Galib Muhammad Shahriar Himel, Md. Aslam Uddin, Hui Liu, Md. Shafiqul Islam
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One-Pixel Attacks (OPAs) represent one of the most extreme demonstrations of adversarial fragility in deep learning, where modifying a single pixel can reliably induce high-confidence misclassification across domains such as medical diagnosis, autonomous driving, biometrics, and quantum communication. Despite their conceptual simplicity, OPAs remain underexamined in existing adversarial-attack surveys, which provide only fragmented or cursory coverage. This PRISMA-guided review synthesizes high-quality studies from 2017 to 2026 and delivers a unified, multi-axis taxonomy of OPA research spanning algorithmic foundations, black-box evolutionary optimization, emerging hybrid and program-synthesis attacks, defence mechanisms, interpretability tools, and domain-specific vulnerabilities. Our analysis reveals the dominance of Differential Evolution-based strategies, the rise of efficiency-optimized and saliency-guided methods, and persistent gaps in dataset diversity, transferability, and standardized evaluation. We summarized and assess defence paradigms including pixel restoration, anomaly detection, input-space transformations, and robust training highlighting their trade-offs in robustness, imperceptibility, and computational overhead. Building on these insights, we outline future research priorities involving selective pixel recovery, transformer-specific vulnerability analysis, saliency-driven optimization, and real-world domain-adaptive defences. We further propose a regulatory framework emphasizing robustness testing, incident disclosure, and AI security governance. This review establishes a comprehensive foundation for understanding, evaluating, and mitigating ultra-sparse adversarial threats in contemporary AI systems.
tldr: This PRISMA-guided review comprehensively surveys one-pixel adversarial attacks on deep learning systems, presenting a taxonomy, defence mechanisms, applications, and regulatory proposals.
motivation: One-pixel attacks expose extreme adversarial fragility in deep learning, yet existing surveys cover them only fragmentarily, motivating a unified review across domains from medical diagnosis to quantum communication.
method: The authors systematically synthesize high-quality studies from 2017 to 2026 using PRISMA guidelines and construct a multi-axis taxonomy spanning algorithmic foundations, black-box optimization, hybrid attacks, defences, interpretability, and domain-specific vulnerabilities.
result: The review finds that Differential Evolution strategies dominate, efficiency-optimized and saliency-guided methods are rising, and persistent gaps remain in dataset diversity, transferability, and standardized evaluation; defence paradigms are compared by robustness, imperceptibility, and computational overhead.
conclusion: The paper establishes a foundational reference for understanding and mitigating ultra-sparse adversarial threats, proposing future directions and an AI security governance framework with robustness testing and incident disclosure.

title: UnifiedAttack: Evaluating The Safety Of Large Multimodal Models In Synergistic Harmful Image-Text Generation
authors: Bingjun Luo, Jialin Guo, Tony Wang, Siqi Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00341v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) transition toward natively unified architectures, evaluating their safety in synergistic harmful image-text generation tasks becomes a critical challenge. Unlike unimodal threats, synergistic risks emerge when text and image modalities are coordinated to produce harm that significantly exceeds their individual components. We introduce UnifiedAttack, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate LMM safety in collaborative scenarios by focusing on the harmfulness gain achieved through cross-modal synergy. The benchmark incorporates samples filtered for their multimodal potential alongside a novel subset of synthesized disinformation queries. To verify identified vulnerabilities, we propose a synergistic hijacking framework featuring In-Context Reskinning (ICR) and Cognitive Planning Injection (CPI). ICR utilizes few-shot learning to wrap adversarial intent in benign virtual shells to desensitize safety filters, while CPI hijacks the reasoning path by enforcing a plan-then-execute paradigm. By compelling the system to commit to a neutral logical plan, we exploit its internal drive for consistency to induce the synchronized generation of harmful multimodal content. Extensive evaluations on state-of-the-art architectures demonstrate that UnifiedAttack consistently bypasses modern alignment. Our findings reveal that the structural helpfulness and logical coherence of unified models can be systematically weaponized, highlighting the urgent need for logic-aware defenses in synergistic generation tasks. Code is available at [URL] .
tldr: UnifiedAttack is a benchmark and attack framework for evaluating the safety of Large Multimodal Models against synergistic harmful image-text generation.
motivation: As LMMs move toward natively unified architectures, harm can arise from coordinated text-image synergy that exceeds unimodal threats, yet existing safety evaluations neglect this cross-modal harmfulness gain.
method: The authors build a benchmark of multimodal-potential samples plus synthesized disinformation queries, and propose a synergistic hijacking framework combining In-Context Reskinning (few-shot benign shells) and Cognitive Planning Injection (plan-then-execute reasoning hijacking).
result: Extensive evaluations show UnifiedAttack consistently bypasses modern alignment across state-of-the-art unified models, exposing logic- and consistency-driven vulnerabilities.
conclusion: The helpfulness and logical coherence of unified models can be systematically weaponized, motivating logic-aware defenses for synergistic multimodal generation.

title: ZoneClaw: Mitigating Persistent Memory Attacks By Establishing Memory-Zoning In OpenClaw-Style Computer-Use Agents
authors: Haokai Ma, Chieh Lin, Yupeng Qiu, Ee-Chien Chang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer-use agents increasingly operate as long-running assistants through persistent workspace memory, which OpenClaw-style CUAs realize as automatically reloaded files that hold user instructions, system summaries, and external claims at the same privilege level. Here, remembering a claim confers authority over later behavior. This enables a persistent memory attack, in which an attacker who controls only benign-looking external content induces the CUA to record attacker-favored claims during a legitimate task, and those claims later govern benign tasks the attacker never touches. The attack chain extends "malicious context -> malicious response" into "malicious context -> memory injection -> malicious execution", making this a cross-environment threat. Existing defenses studied intervene either before content enters memory or at the action it later induces, not whether stored content may guide action. We propose ZoneClaw, which separates persistence from authority by replacing flat workspace memory with hierarchical trust zones carrying explicit authority levels. External claims persist in a low-trust zone and acquire action-guiding authority only by crossing an explicit authority boundary, at which promotion is cross-checked against zones the attacker cannot directly write. Role-specific processes of asymmetric privilege enforce this boundary, ensuring that no process both ingests external content and acts outward. Across four attack scenarios, two injection settings, and four backbones, ZoneClaw drives ASR from 372/480 to 6/480 while retaining utility in 458/480 trials, and remains effective against some defense-aware attackers. Attacker claims still persist in low-trust memory yet rarely cross the authority boundary, showing that ZoneClaw withholds authority rather than refusing to learn from the environment. Our code is available at: [URL].
tldr: ZoneClaw defends OpenClaw-style computer-use agents against persistent memory attacks by replacing flat workspace memory with hierarchical trust zones and explicit authority levels.
motivation: Persistent workspace memory can grant external attacker-controlled claims the same privilege as user instructions, enabling a malicious context to be remembered and later executed in benign tasks.
method: It separates persistence from authority: external claims are stored in a low-trust zone and can guide action only after crossing an authority boundary, enforced by role-specific processes of asymmetric privilege.
result: Across four attack scenarios, two injection settings, and four backbones, ZoneClaw reduces attack success rate from 372/480 to 6/480 while retaining utility in 458/480 trials.
conclusion: ZoneClaw shows that low-trust memory can persist without acquiring action-guiding authority, withstanding some defense-aware attackers by withholding authority rather than refusing to learn.

title: Identity-Bound Governance Under Execution Uncertainty: An Accountability Proof Block For Llm Agent Persistent Halts, With Cryptographic Implementation And Cross-Model Calibration
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A correctly governed LLM agent can reach a state in which neither continuing execution nor automatically halting is admissible: the system has detected a persistent failure of its observability or drift-detection layer, but cannot itself decide who has the authority to resume, deny, or recalibrate the deployment. We call this an identity-bound governance event and formalise the mechanism that resolves it. We introduce the Accountability Proof Block (APB): a system-constructed evidence block, a human-supplied decision block, and an ed25519 signature binding both to a registered principal. The system cannot forge the signature, and the principal cannot alter the evidence undetected. We prove four theorems: Protocol-Bounded Governance Completeness, Non-Repudiability, Impossibility of Anonymous Re-Authorization, and Finite-Time APB Construction Termination. The implementation uses RFC 8785 JSON canonicalization and a UUID4-based replay predicate. Empirically, governance completeness holds over 3,812 halt events with zero unresolved cases; the verifier detects 100% of 1,800 attacks across 9 adversarial vectors; a k-of-n multi-principal variant shows 0 false acceptances in 2,000 single-key capture attempts. A study of six open LLMs finds the drift threshold T* stable within model (sigma/T* < 2%) but varying across models, refuting size-monotonicity: the largest model did not drift. T* must therefore be measured per deployment, and the APB is the vehicle by which that threshold yields accountable authority transfer.
tldr: The paper introduces an Accountability Proof Block (APB) for resolving identity-bound governance events in LLM agent deployments using cryptographic signatures and a human decision block.
motivation: LLM agents can reach states where continued execution and automatic halting are both inadmissible, requiring a formal mechanism for accountable authority transfer.
method: The authors formalize an APB composed of a system-constructed evidence block, a human-supplied decision block, and an ed25519 signature binding both to a registered principal, proving four governance theorems and implementing it with RFC 8785 JSON canonicalization and a UUID4 replay predicate.
result: The implementation achieves governance completeness over 3,812 halt events with zero unresolved cases, detects 100% of 1,800 attacks across 9 vectors, and shows stable within-model drift thresholds but non-monotonic cross-model variation.
conclusion: Accountable authority transfer for LLM agents can be cryptographically enforced, but the drift threshold T* must be measured per deployment rather than inferred from model size.

title: AuraForge: Scaling Security Supervision For Training Coding Agents
authors: Danqing Wang, Songwen Zhao, Harsh Sharma, Jierui Wang, Andre Vicente Duarte, Ivan Bercovich, Lei Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00850v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents are now proficient enough to generate complex software applications from a single prompt. As their capabilities have grown, human oversight has increasingly shifted from line-by-line code review toward hands-off evaluation of outcomes. However, recent studies have shown that such a transition exposes a critical risk: functional correctness alone does not guarantee a secure implementation. Despite growing attention to code security, training safer coding agents remains challenging because reliable security supervision is difficult to obtain at scale from real-world repositories. We introduce AuraForge to synthesize and validate executable security tests for training secure coding agents. Our approach combines attack-oriented test synthesis, language-extensible task construction, and safeguards against reward hacking. Using AuraForge, we construct AuraGym, a multi-language and multi-CWE executable training gym: 679 executable feature-implementation tasks from 344 real-world repositories across Python, JavaScript, and TypeScript, covering 177 CWE categories. On the subset with human-written security tests, AuraForge produces about 3 times as many test cases on average and reduces the false-positive rate by 83.23%, allowing alternative secure implementations to receive correct supervision. Training Qwen3.5-4B with synthesized security tests gains larger improvements than human-written security tests (average 19.7 FuncPass and 6.2 SecPass vs. 14.9 FuncPass and 4.4 SecPass) on three languages. These results demonstrate that AuraForge provides more diverse and reliable security supervision to train secure coding agents.
tldr: AuraForge synthesizes and validates executable security tests to train coding agents, producing the AuraGym multi-language benchmark and improving secure-code training over human-written tests.
motivation: As coding agents move from line-by-line review to outcome-based evaluation, functional correctness no longer guarantees security, yet scalable and reliable security supervision data from real repositories is scarce.
method: The framework combines attack-oriented test synthesis, language-extensible task construction, and safeguards against reward hacking to generate executable security tests across Python, JavaScript, and TypeScript.
result: AuraForge yields roughly 3x more test cases on human-tested subsets with an 83.23% reduction in false positives, and training Qwen3.5-4B with synthesized tests improves FuncPass (19.7) and SecPass (6.2) over human-written tests (14.9/4.4) across three languages.
conclusion: Synthesized security supervision provides more diverse and reliable signals than human-written tests, enabling safer code-generation agents.

title: Momat: Mixture Of Multiple Atlases For Low-Power Jailbreak Defense Of Quantized LLMs
authors: Boyang Li, Bingyu Shen, Weihao Hong, Zhiyuan Jiang, Xinlei Guan, Yan Ma, Miles Q. Li, Yi Sheng, Ruiyang Qin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.01058v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantized large language models are increasingly deployed on edge devices for their low latency and energy efficiency. However, model quantization weakens alignment safeguards, leaving qLLMs (quantized large language models) highly vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. To address this challenge, we present MOMAT (Mixture of Multiple Atlases), a hardware-enhanced safety framework that combines structured knowledge retrieval with low-power defense acceleration. Each atlas represents a semantic cluster of harmful or benign sample sets and policy templates, enabling domain-localized Retrieval-Augmented Generation guarding that mitigates the curse of dimensionality and the resulting semantic sparsity problem in large, heterogeneous safety databases. MOMAT retrieves top-[MATH] similarity features from all atlases for each prompt and evaluates them using a lightweight MoE (Mixture of Experts) detector, while a CiM (Compute-in-Memory)-accelerated similarity engine performs fast, low-power atlas-local retrieval. MOMAT's CiM-based retrieval accelerates a 100-query batch from 15,052.44 ms to 3,207.21 ns (a [MATH] speedup) and reduces energy from [MATH] [MATH]J to 3.32 [MATH]J, yielding an approximately [MATH] energy reduction over DRAM-based (Raspberry Pi) baselines. Red-team evaluations across standard benchmarks show that MOMAT matches the defense performance of state-of-the-art methods while avoiding benign overkill and providing substantial efficiency gains, demonstrating that CiM-based modular defenses can make edge-deployed qLLMs both safer and more energy-efficient. We will release the full 223.2k-sample dataset to foster future research.
tldr: MOMAT is a hardware-enhanced safety framework that combines multiple semantic atlases and compute-in-memory acceleration to defend quantized LLMs against jailbreak attacks with low power consumption.
motivation: Quantized LLMs deployed on edge devices are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks because quantization weakens alignment safeguards, and existing defenses are either computationally expensive or ineffective for resource-constrained settings.
method: MOMAT clusters harmful and benign samples and policy templates into multiple atlases, retrieves top-M similarity features from each atlas, and uses a lightweight Mixture-of-Experts detector alongside a Compute-in-Memory similarity engine for fast, low-power atlas-local retrieval.
result: MOMAT accelerates a 100-query batch from 15,052.44 ms to 3,207.21 ns and reduces energy from millijoules to 3.32 microjoules, achieving roughly a thousand-fold energy reduction over DRAM-based baselines while matching state-of-the-art defense performance without benign overkill.
conclusion: CiM-based modular defenses can make edge-deployed quantized LLMs both safer and more energy-efficient, and the authors plan to release a 223.2k-sample dataset to support future research.

title: Adaptivity, Anchoring, And The Exact Oracle Complexity Of Stochastic Fixed-Point Iterations
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study stochastic fixed-point iterations [MATH] for nonexpansive and contractive operators on Hilbert spaces, with a single-point unbiased oracle of bounded variance. Deterministically, every anchor schedule [MATH] whose density [MATH] does not oscillate between scales is either polynomially suboptimal on contractions or super-polynomially slow on rotations; for constant densities [MATH] the tradeoff is exact, with [MATH] on rotations by angle [MATH] ([MATH], [MATH]) and, for the classical schedule, [MATH]. The dichotomy fails exactly under lacunary anchor concentration: an explicit [MATH]-oblivious schedule, one per target accuracy, is simultaneously contraction-optimal and rotation-polynomial with exponent [MATH], [MATH], and, for each fixed target accuracy, the matching lower bound holds for Lebesgue-a.e.\ angle. For stochastic contractions, the minimax rate is [MATH] on affine maps, and within the anchored class [MATH] for known modulus via geometric batching; without a certified modulus bound no sound distance certificate exists, and a certified ceiling is the exact boundary. For nonexpansive maps we prove [MATH] in every [MATH]-uniformly smooth Banach space and the Hilbert rate [MATH] by reduction to monotone inclusions. Numerical experiments are consistent with every scaling prediction.
tldr: The paper analyzes the exact oracle complexity of stochastic fixed-point iterations for nonexpansive and contractive operators on Hilbert spaces, focusing on anchor schedules and adaptivity.
motivation: Stochastic fixed-point iterations are fundamental in optimization and monotone inclusion problems, and their oracle complexity tradeoffs under different anchor schedules are not fully understood.
method: The authors study deterministic and stochastic oracle models, derive lower and upper bounds for contraction and rotation operators, and introduce lacunary anchor concentration schedules.
result: They prove exact complexities for constant density anchors, show a dichotomy under lacunary concentration, and establish minimax rates for affine contractions and nonexpansive maps in uniformly smooth Banach spaces.
conclusion: The work provides tight oracle complexity characterizations for stochastic fixed-point iterations, supported by numerical experiments, but it is purely mathematical optimization without quantum information or thermodynamics content.

title: The Five-Point Case Of Mordell's Discriminant Inequality
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] satisfy [MATH]. We prove the sharp inequality \[ \prod_{1\le i<j\le5}|z_i-z_j|^2\le 5^5, \] with equality precisely for a regular pentagon on the unit circle, up to rotation and permutation. This settles the remaining five-point case of the discriminant problem considered by Mordell in 1960. The proof first identifies a maximizer with a normalized relative equilibrium of five identical planar point vortices. We then give an independent exact classification of the corresponding stationary equations. The main algebraic step proves that every collision-free physical solution of the normalized stationary equations is reflection symmetric; it is obtained from a resultant construction and exact Gr\"obner-basis elimination over [MATH]. The reflection-symmetric equations have exactly five physical shapes, and an exact discriminant comparison selects the regular pentagon. All symbolic eliminations, Sturm counts, and interval inequalities are reproduced by an accompanying verification script using rational arithmetic. As consequences, the same configuration gives the Gaussian weighted Fekete set and the global mode of the five-particle complex Ginibre density after the natural rescaling.
tldr: The paper proves the sharp five-point case of Mordell's discriminant inequality, showing the maximum is attained only by the regular pentagon on the unit circle.
motivation: Mordell posed the discriminant inequality problem in 1960, and the five-point case had remained open; this work aims to settle that remaining case.
method: The proof identifies a maximizer with a normalized relative equilibrium of five planar point vortices, then classifies the stationary equations using resultants, Gröbner-basis elimination, Sturm counts, and exact interval inequalities verified by a rational-arithmetic script.
result: Every collision-free physical solution of the normalized stationary equations is reflection symmetric, and the reflection-symmetric equations yield exactly five physical shapes, among which the regular pentagon is selected by discriminant comparison.
conclusion: The regular pentagon configuration also gives the Gaussian weighted Fekete set and the global mode of the five-particle complex Ginibre density after natural rescaling.

title: The Cognitive Continuity Test: Verifying Governed State Transitions In Persistent Ai Agents
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00132v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Persistent AI agents revise beliefs, consolidate memory, and replace execution substrates. Similar successor states can accompany differently authorized transition claims, while legitimate development can change state substantially. We introduce the Cognitive Continuity Test (CCT), a policy-relative contract for verifying submitted transitions using scoped authority, provenance, deterministic application, semantic predicates, and candidate-persistence receipts. CCT distinguishes verified admissibility, affirmative violation, and unresolved required evidence. Separation results concern transition claims rather than live runtime identity; soundness is conditional on the specified checker and evaluator assumptions. IdentityLineageBench provides 24 generated transition families. The reference post-resolution verifier matches all 576 canonical held-out labels; lexical state similarity and a lineage-only diagnostic baseline admit 60.0% and 80.0% of invalid fixtures. These comparisons establish synthetic conformance, not superiority to a policy-aware deployed system. Signed adversarial regressions cover fabricated interaction counts, unsupported belief changes, and mixed missing/contradictory evidence. SIT behavior and actual model migration remain unmeasured. An 18,000-execution valid-path study measures a 6.21 ms default median on resident inputs. We specify the additional activation and recovery obligations needed for deployment.
tldr: The paper introduces the Cognitive Continuity Test (CCT), a policy-relative verification contract for validating governed state transitions in persistent AI agents, with a synthetic benchmark and verifier evaluation.
motivation: Persistent AI agents frequently revise beliefs, consolidate memory, and change execution substrates, creating a need to distinguish legitimate state transitions from unauthorized or inconsistent ones.
method: CCT uses scoped authority, provenance, deterministic application, semantic predicates, and candidate-persistence receipts to verify transition claims, separating verified admissibility, affirmative violation, and unresolved required evidence.
result: The reference post-resolution verifier matches all 576 canonical held-out labels, while lexical state similarity and a lineage-only baseline admit 60.0% and 80.0% of invalid fixtures, respectively; an 18,000-execution valid-path study reports a 6.21 ms default median on resident inputs.
conclusion: The work establishes synthetic conformance for CCT but does not demonstrate superiority over policy-aware deployed systems, and SIT behavior and actual model migration remain unmeasured.

title: On The Relationship Between Model Quantization And Model Inversion Attacks
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00382v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model quantization reduces the numerical precision of neural network weights and activations to lower storage and computational costs. Model inversion attacks recover or reconstruct sensitive training data or inference inputs from model outputs or intermediate features, so quantization may also alter their effectiveness. However, two questions remain unresolved: How does model quantization affect model inversion? How do data characteristics influence this relationship? To address the first, we bound quantization-induced changes in mutual information between inputs and a categorical variable defined by prediction probabilities, distinguishing informational effects from attack optimization obstacles. To address the second, we identify data-dependent changes in feature distributions and inversion outcomes, with pronounced quantization sensitivity differences at 4 bits. These insights guide a privacy-aware post-training quantization method that improves inversion resistance while recovering utility. It uses a Fisher-type task-sensitivity proxy for budget-aware bit allocation, calibrates activation ranges, and jointly optimizes weight and activation scales and weight-rounding decisions with task-recovery and geometry-retention objectives and scale and rounding regularization. Experiments cover multiple metrics, neural network architectures, and face, palmprint, and iris recognition tasks. On ResNet-50, Palm at 4 bits reduces RL-MIA's strict success from 54% to 26%, while accuracy decreases from 99.01% to 96.55% relative to FP32. Our method also supports output-level defenses: adding Stealthy Shield Defense (SSD, epsilon = 0.1) to Iris at 4.5 bits reduces BREP-MI's strict success from 63.33% to 37.33%, while accuracy decreases from 92.8% to 87.6% relative to quantization alone.
tldr: This paper analyzes how model quantization affects model inversion attacks in neural networks and proposes a privacy-aware post-training quantization method that improves inversion resistance while retaining utility.
motivation: Quantization lowers numerical precision to reduce storage and computation, but its impact on model inversion attacks that reconstruct sensitive training data or inputs remains unresolved, especially regarding data-dependent effects.
method: The authors bound quantization-induced changes in mutual information between inputs and a categorical prediction-probability variable, and analyze data-dependent feature distribution shifts. They then design a privacy-aware post-training quantization approach using a Fisher-type task-sensitivity proxy for bit allocation and joint optimization of weight/activation scales and rounding decisions.
result: Experiments on face, palmprint, and iris recognition show improved inversion resistance: on ResNet-50 with Palm at 4 bits, RL-MIA strict success drops from 54% to 26% while accuracy falls from 99.01% to 96.55% relative to FP32; adding SSD to Iris at 4.5 bits reduces BREP-MI strict success from 63.33% to 37.33% with accuracy 92.8% to 87.6%.
conclusion: Quantization can meaningfully alter model inversion vulnerability in a data-dependent way, and carefully designed quantization can serve as a privacy defense with manageable utility loss.

title: Matching Lower Bounds For Randomized First-Order Methods In Hessian-Lipschitz Nonconvex Optimization
authors: Haihan Zhang, Wendao Wu, Chenheng Zhang, Yanyi Li, Chunyuan Zheng, Cong Fang, Haoxuan Li, Zhouchen Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a randomized first-order lower bound for finding an [MATH]-stationary point, [MATH], of a nonconvex function with initial gap at most [MATH], [MATH]-Lipschitz gradient, and [MATH]-Lipschitz Hessian. Each oracle call returns the exact function value and gradient. Let [MATH] denote the minimax number of calls, maximized over finite dimensions, for arbitrary adaptive randomized algorithms with per-instance success probability at least [MATH]. In the regime [MATH] and [MATH], we prove [MATH] where [MATH] is an absolute constant. This matches the deterministic restarted accelerated-gradient upper bound of Li and Lin (2023) and extends the sharp deterministic lower bound of Zhou (2026) to unrestricted randomized algorithms. Thus, randomization does not improve the high-dimensional worst-case query rate. The construction keeps quadratic curvature visible while revealing the forcing directions sequentially. Large eigenspaces limit preprocessing, and a scheduled-disclosure coupling makes each fresh direction incur a separate cost.
tldr: The paper proves a randomized first-order oracle lower bound for finding approximate stationary points of nonconvex Hessian-Lipschitz functions, matching the deterministic accelerated-gradient upper bound and showing randomization gives no improvement in high dimensions.
motivation: Worst-case query-complexity lower bounds for nonconvex optimization have largely been established for deterministic algorithms, leaving open whether randomization can beat them in the Hessian-Lipschitz setting.
method: The authors construct a hard instance family with large eigenspaces that limit preprocessing and use a scheduled-disclosure coupling so that each newly revealed forcing direction incurs a separate query cost, yielding a minimax argument over adaptive randomized algorithms.
result: In the regime of large initial gap and small target accuracy, the minimax number of oracle calls is bounded below by an expression matching the deterministic restarted accelerated-gradient upper bound of Li and Lin (2023), extending Zhou's sharp deterministic lower bound to unrestricted randomized algorithms.
conclusion: Randomization does not improve the high-dimensional worst-case query rate for this class of nonconvex problems, closing the gap between randomized lower bounds and deterministic upper bounds.

title: Safety In Self-Evolving Agents: A Survey
authors: Jiahao Chen, Zhou Feng, Oubo Ma, Yichen Yan, Ruixiao Lin, Hangtao Zhang, Linkang Du, Hengyu An, Yong Yang, Jun Liu, Junhao Li, Naen Xu, Chunyi Zhou, Yuan Su, Zehao Jin, Qianli Ma, Leyi Qi, Yiming Wang, Zhe Ma, Yuwen Pu, Mengyao Du, Yuanyi Song, Enhao Huang, Zhihui Fu, Jun Wang, Jinfeng Li, Yuefeng Chen, Hui Xue, Yiming Li, Tianyu Du, Shouling Ji
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong general capabilities, yet their parameters typically remain fixed after deployment, limiting learning from new interactions. In open-ended environments, this motivates self-evolving agents that continually update reusable state-including model parameters, memories, tool definitions, skills, and workflows-from data, feedback, and accumulated experience. This shift changes the safety problem: once experience becomes reusable state, past events become future causes, and information harmless in one context may later influence decisions with greater persistence, authority, or scope. Self-evolving agent safety therefore asks not only whether a response is aligned or an action authorized, but whether safety properties survive the accumulation, generalization, and cross-context reuse of locally useful experience. We introduce SAVER, a transition-centered framework in which Substrate locates reusable influence, Adaptation captures how it changes, Violation identifies compromised safety attributes, Exposure marks where failures become observable, and Response assesses containment, repair, or revocation. Our survey reveals that failures need not originate from harmful information: legitimate state can become unsafe when adaptation expands its persistence, authority, or scope beyond the conditions under which it was valid. Existing work provides comparatively strong evidence for admission, retrieval, activation, exposure, and local containment, but much less for descendant repair and evaluation after adaptation resumes. We therefore argue for longitudinal evaluation that traces unsafe influence to its originating transition, verifies repair across descendants, and tests whether it can re-emerge under continued evolution.
tldr: SAVER is a transition-centered survey framework for understanding safety failures in self-evolving LLM agents whose reusable state (parameters, memory, tools, skills) can turn benign experience into persistent, cross-context unsafe influence.
motivation: LLM parameters are fixed after deployment, motivating self-evolving agents that continually update reusable state from data, feedback, and experience; this shift makes past events become future causes and demands safety notions beyond per-response alignment or action authorization.
method: The authors propose the SAVER framework decomposing self-evolving agent safety into Substrate (locus of reusable influence), Adaptation (how it changes), Violation (compromised safety attributes), Exposure (observability of failures), and Response (containment, repair, revocation), and survey existing work along these dimensions.
result: The survey finds relatively strong evidence for admission, retrieval, activation, exposure, and local containment, but much weaker coverage of descendant repair and evaluation after adaptation resumes, showing failures can arise from legitimate state rather than harmful information.
conclusion: The authors argue for longitudinal evaluation that traces unsafe influence back to its originating transition, verifies repair across descendants, and tests whether unsafe behavior can re-emerge under continued evolution.

title: Migration Flows: Population Scaling And Heavy Tails
authors: Cook Hyun Kim, Sangjoon Park, Seoyoung Jin, Jaiyong Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show how migration between counties in different cities can explain both the population scaling of mean intercity flows and heavy-tailed intercity net-flow distributions. Density-dependent departure and arrival activities determine how mean flows scale with the populations of the origin and destination cities. We assume Gaussian county-pair net flows with standard deviations proportional to their mean directional flows. At a fixed correlation between county-pair net flows, their sum is Gaussian. Averaging this conditional Gaussian density over the correlation distribution can produce an intermediate power law with a Gaussian cutoff. We also present a stochastic model that generates the variance distribution used in this mixture.
tldr: A stochastic and scaling model explains intercity migration flows by aggregating county-level density-dependent Gaussian flows, yielding power-law mean scaling and heavy-tailed net-flow distributions.
motivation: Intercity migration exhibits both population scaling of mean flows and heavy-tailed net-flow distributions, but a unified mechanistic explanation from county-level dynamics is lacking.
method: The authors assume county-pair net flows are Gaussian with standard deviations proportional to mean directional flows, derive conditional Gaussian sums, and average over a correlation distribution generated by a stochastic model.
result: The aggregation produces an intermediate power law with Gaussian cutoff in net-flow distributions, while density-dependent departure/arrival activities determine how mean flows scale with origin and destination populations.
conclusion: County-level migration dynamics can jointly account for population scaling and heavy-tailed intercity net flows, linking microscopic stochastic rules to macroscopic flow statistics.

title: Inverse Optimal Control With Convex Features And Box Constraints
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00033v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study an inverse optimal-control problem for identifying nonnegative weights in a convex-feature lower-level objective. The resulting model is an optimistic bilevel optimal-control problem whose lower level is a strongly convex, linearly constrained control problem with box constraints in \(L^2\). For the reduced response map \(x\mapsto (y_x,u_x)\), we prove global single-valuedness and an explicit Lipschitz estimate, without assuming differentiability of active sets. Exploiting the affine dependence of the lower-level functional on \(x\), we show that the value function is concave and Lipschitz and derive an asymptotically exact optimal-value relaxation. We further establish local identifiability and \(O(\delta)\) noise stability by a gradient-free argument based on second-order growth. Finally, a KKT reformulation yields a function-space MPCC; Scholtes relaxation gives C-stationarity under uniform multiplier boundedness. A decoupled scalar example provides an explicit strict-complementarity certificate via finiteness of threshold contacts.
tldr: The paper studies inverse optimal control for identifying nonnegative weights in a convex-feature lower-level objective with box constraints, establishing theoretical properties of the resulting bilevel optimal-control problem.
motivation: The authors aim to recover unknown objective weights from observed behavior in a control setting where the lower-level problem is strongly convex and box-constrained.
method: They formulate an optimistic bilevel optimal-control problem, prove Lipschitz continuity and single-valuedness of the response map, derive a concave value function and an asymptotically exact relaxation, and analyze identifiability, noise stability, and a KKT-based MPCC reformulation.
result: They obtain global single-valuedness, explicit Lipschitz estimates, local identifiability with O(delta) noise stability, and C-stationarity under uniform multiplier boundedness, plus an explicit strict-complementarity certificate in a scalar example.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous foundations for inverse optimal control with convex features and box constraints, but it is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Minimal Control Time Of Some 1d First-order Linear Hyperbolic Systems With Row Rank Deficient Boundary Coupling Matrix
authors: Long Hu, Guillaume Olive, Zengzhi Xin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The minimal control time of one-dimensional first-order linear hyperbolic systems is by now well-known when the boundary coupling matrix is full row rank. The goal of this article is to characterize the minimal control time for a class of systems with row rank deficient boundary coupling matrices.
tldr: The paper characterizes the minimal control time for one-dimensional first-order linear hyperbolic systems whose boundary coupling matrix is row rank deficient, extending classical results valid only for full row rank cases.
motivation: Minimal control time for 1D first-order linear hyperbolic systems is well understood when the boundary coupling matrix has full row rank, but the row rank deficient case lacks a general characterization.
method: The authors analyze boundary control of one-dimensional first-order linear hyperbolic PDE systems, deriving conditions on the coupling matrix structure to determine minimal control times in the rank-deficient regime.
result: A characterization of the minimal control time for a class of systems with row rank deficient boundary coupling matrices is established, generalizing prior full-rank results.
conclusion: The work fills a gap in the controllability theory of hyperbolic systems, providing minimal control time formulas for rank-deficient boundary couplings.

title: Sharpness And Rigidity Of The Two-Factor Recht-Re Lower Bound
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Products of positive semidefinite matrices arise when successive steps of a randomized optimization method use different data points. Their average can have a negative eigenvalue even though every individual matrix is positive semidefinite. Lai and Lim proved at ICML 2020 that [MATH] whenever [MATH] and [MATH], and conjectured that the constant is sharp for every [MATH]. We give an explicit family of [MATH] rank-one matrices in dimension [MATH] that attains this bound for every [MATH], proving that sharpness statement. The construction compresses one direction of an orthonormal basis by a factor [MATH]. We also give a short, self-contained proof of the known inequality and classify all equality cases: every extremizer contains a common invariant [MATH]-dimensional block equivalent to the construction. Consequently, dimension [MATH] is necessary for equality, and positive definite matrices approach but never attain the lower endpoint. Finally, strongly convex quadratic objectives realize the extremal negative eigenvalue as a two-step expected gradient-descent update.
tldr: The paper proves sharpness and characterizes equality cases for the two-factor Recht-Re lower bound on the minimum eigenvalue of averaged positive semidefinite matrices.
motivation: Products and averages of positive semidefinite matrices arise in randomized optimization and can have negative eigenvalues despite each matrix being positive semidefinite; the sharp constant in the known lower bound was conjectured but not proven.
method: The author constructs an explicit family of rank-one matrices attaining the bound and gives a self-contained proof of the inequality, then classifies all equality cases via invariant block structure.
result: The construction achieves the conjectured bound for every dimension and shows that equality requires a common invariant 2-dimensional block; positive definite matrices approach but do not attain the endpoint.
conclusion: The sharpness conjecture is confirmed, and the extremal behavior is realized in strongly convex quadratic objectives as a two-step expected gradient-descent update.

title: A Two-Dimensional Extremizer For Relatively Inexact Gradient Descent
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give an explicit extremal function for one step of gradient descent when the gradient error is bounded relative to the true gradient. The function is the sum of a quadratic in one coordinate and a Huber function in the other. It attains, for every admissible relative error level and every stepsize in the intermediate regime, the proposed worst-case constants for both the final squared gradient divided by the initial objective gap and the final squared gradient divided by the objective decrease. This proves Conjecture 2.6 of Vernimmen and Glineur, first stated in June 2025. A change of variable reduces the parameter description to a scalar cubic with a rigorously specified root. We prove all parameter inequalities, derive a nonnegative-square certificate for the upper bound, and verify the matching construction directly. We also characterize the exact one-dimensional worst-case value and prove that two dimensions are necessary in the open intermediate regime.
tldr: The paper constructs a two-dimensional extremal function proving worst-case bounds for relatively inexact gradient descent, confirming a conjecture of Vernimmen and Glineur.
motivation: Understanding convergence guarantees of gradient descent under relative gradient error is important for optimization theory, and a conjectured worst-case extremizer was previously unresolved.
method: The authors give an explicit extremal function as a sum of a quadratic and a Huber function, reduce parameters to a scalar cubic root, prove parameter inequalities, and derive a nonnegative-square certificate.
result: The proposed worst-case constants for final squared gradient divided by initial objective gap and by objective decrease are attained for every admissible relative error and intermediate stepsize; two dimensions are necessary in the open intermediate regime.
conclusion: The work proves Conjecture 2.6 of Vernimmen and Glineur and provides a rigorous characterization of the one-dimensional worst-case value, settling the problem.

title: Certificate-Coupled Dca For The Trust-Region Subproblem: Early Structural Escape And Progressive Global Certification
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the nonconvex trust-region subproblem by a certificate-coupled difference-of-convex algorithm that incorporates spectral information before exact first-order stationarity is attained. The method maintains a persistent randomized Krylov subspace together with the DCA iterates. Near stationarity, a sufficiently negative shifted Rayleigh quotient yields an explicit feasible correction with a quantitative decrease in the objective value; otherwise, completion of a prescribed Lanczos depth provides, with high probability, an approximate positive-semidefiniteness certificate. The same Krylov subspace also provides a certified upper bound on the largest eigenvalue for selecting the DC curvature parameter at subsequent accuracy stages. We prove a uniform negative-curvature correction result over the trust region, covering the near-orthogonal hard-case regime, together with finite-termination and work bounds at fixed tolerances and a quantitative objective-gap certificate. Under a progressive accuracy schedule, the certified objective values converge to the global optimum and the iterates converge in distance to the global solution set, while the Krylov subspace is retained across corrections and accuracy stages. Numerical experiments illustrate the phenomena established by the analysis: negative-curvature corrections can occur before the corresponding post-convergence spectral corrections, the quantitative decrease bound is satisfied in all tested near-orthogonal instances, and retaining the Krylov subspace reduces the median number of spectral matrix-vector products by approximately a factor of [MATH] relative to restarting the spectral process in the controlled comparison.
tldr: A certificate-coupled difference-of-convex algorithm using a persistent randomized Krylov subspace is developed for the nonconvex trust-region subproblem, with early negative-curvature corrections and progressive global certification.
motivation: The nonconvex trust-region subproblem is hard because first-order stationarity does not guarantee global optimality, and spectral information is typically only used after convergence; the authors aim to exploit it earlier.
method: The algorithm couples DCA iterates with a randomized Krylov/Lanczos subspace, using shifted Rayleigh quotient negativity for feasible corrections and Lanczos depth completion for PSD certificates, while reusing the subspace across stages to bound the largest eigenvalue.
result: Uniform negative-curvature correction results (including the near-orthogonal hard case), finite-termination and work bounds, and a quantitative objective-gap certificate are proven; experiments show early spectral escape and ~1/factor reduction in median spectral matvecs.
conclusion: Under a progressive accuracy schedule the certified objective values and iterates converge to the global optimum and solution set, indicating a practical and certifiable method for nonconvex trust-region problems.

title: Data-to-Certificates (d2c): Koopman Supereigenfunctions For Stability, Safety, And Control
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional dynamical system models, including Koopman operator representations, are fundamentally equality-based, whereas many analysis and control tools rely on inequalities. This mismatch motivates representations that are intrinsically aligned with certification tasks involved in the analysis and control synthesis problems. In this paper, we propose a paradigm that bypasses explicit model construction and directly learns certificates from data. We introduce of the Koopman operator as an inequality-based generalization of eigenfunctions that define exponential growth envelopes encoding stability, safety, and uncertainty propagation, thereby serving as certificates for a range of control objectives. We establish their theoretical foundations and show that the associated rates recover intrinsic dynamical quantities such as Lyapunov exponents. Two complementary constructions are developed: a geometric approach based on the multiplicative ergodic theorem (MET), and a resolvent/Gramian formulation that enables computation directly from trajectory data. The resulting framework yields certificates that can be used for stability and contraction analysis, as well as stabilizing and safety-critical control synthesis via convex quadratic programming-based optimization program. Numerical examples demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed data-driven certification approach for stabilization, contraction, and safe control design.
tldr: The paper proposes data-to-certificates (d2c) using Koopman supereigenfunctions to directly learn certificates for stability, safety, and control without explicit model construction.
motivation: Traditional Koopman representations are equality-based, while many analysis and control tasks rely on inequalities, motivating certificate representations aligned with certification objectives.
method: It introduces Koopman supereigenfunctions as inequality-based generalizations of eigenfunctions, with geometric and resolvent/Gramian constructions that compute certificates directly from trajectory data.
result: The framework recovers intrinsic dynamical quantities such as Lyapunov exponents and yields certificates usable for stability, contraction analysis, and stabilizing or safety-critical control via convex quadratic programming.
conclusion: Numerical examples demonstrate effective data-driven certification for stabilization, contraction, and safe control design.

title: Gradient-Only Online Convex Optimization With A Single Quadratic Leader
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study online convex optimization on a bounded Euclidean domain when the learner receives only one subgradient at its prediction and knows neither the horizon, a gradient bound, nor the losses' strong-convexity parameters. We present a scale-invariant algorithm that couples projected adaptive gradient descent to one cone-constrained quadratic leader through a positive wealth process. The algorithm maintains [MATH] state, without a learning-rate grid or restarts. For a domain of diameter at most [MATH], it guarantees regret at most [MATH], with no logarithmic factor. A simultaneous quadratic-distance bound yields explicit improvements for unknown strong convexity, including a refinement governed by jumps in the observed gradient scale. For varying per-round curvature, the bound depends on the total shortfall below a reference level selected in hindsight. The proof uses a clipping-compatible surrogate and a potential involving the quadratic minimum, log wealth, and two scalar curvature statistics. The resulting strongly convex bound is not uniform at the classical logarithmic rate over all curvature-to-gradient ratios; the exact parameter dependence is stated. The contribution is a single-leader construction and its analysis, within an established literature on universal and scale-free online learning.
tldr: The paper introduces a scale-invariant online convex optimization algorithm using one subgradient per round and a single cone-constrained quadratic leader to achieve regret bounds without knowing horizon, gradient bound, or strong-convexity parameters.
motivation: Online convex optimization often assumes known problem parameters or requires learning-rate tuning; this work seeks a parameter-free, scale-invariant method with minimal per-round gradient information.
method: The algorithm couples projected adaptive gradient descent with one cone-constrained quadratic leader via a positive wealth process, maintaining a lightweight state and avoiding learning-rate grids or restarts.
result: It guarantees regret at most proportional to the domain diameter with no logarithmic factor, yields a simultaneous quadratic-distance bound, and provides explicit improvements for unknown strong convexity and varying curvature.
conclusion: The contribution is a single-leader construction and analysis within universal and scale-free online learning, refining regret bounds under unknown or varying curvature.

title: Sharp Fresh-Gradient Complexity Of Nonconvex-Strongly-Concave Minimax Optimization

title: Joint Lower Bounds For Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization On Euclidean Balls
authors: Haihan Zhang, Wendao Wu, Chenheng Zhang, Yanyi Li, Chunyuan Zheng, Cong Fang, Haoxuan Li, Zhouchen Lin

title: Sharp Minimax Rates For Highly Smooth Strongly Convex Zeroth-Order Optimization
authors: Haihan Zhang, Wendao Wu, Chenheng Zhang, Yanyi Li, Chunyuan Zheng, Cong Fang, Haoxuan Li, Zhouchen Lin

motivation: Zeroth-order optimization is important when gradients are unavailable, but the minimax dimension dependence for highly smooth and strongly convex functions under noisy function evaluations was not fully understood.
method: The authors derive a lower bound using a localized normalized hypercube argument with a radial cutoff to limit information per query, and construct a self-contained multiscale spherical estimator to match the upper bound.
result: They show the minimax expected objective error scales as a dimension- and budget-dependent rate without logarithmic loss, matching the upper bound of Akhavan et al. (2024) and holding for arbitrary randomized adaptive algorithms.
conclusion: The work closes the gap in minimax rates for noisy zeroth-order optimization with higher-order smoothness and strong convexity, providing tight necessary and sufficient query complexity.

title: Finite-time Boundary Collision In Planar Linear Quadratic Regulator Gradient Flows
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Policy gradient methods for the linear quadratic regulator optimize feedback gains using a cost over an infinite horizon. When this cost is evaluated at one fixed initial state, it need not diverge near every part of the stability boundary. We study whether the Euclidean gradient flow can reach this boundary in finite optimization time. For controllable planar systems with one input and positive definite quadratic weights, an exact representation of the cost yields a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of such a collision. The condition reduces to a scalar root calculation and includes the critical case, where a double direction root attracts an open set of stabilizing gains. For a triangular family, the criterion gives an explicit algebraic parameter region, and every trajectory either converges to the Riccati gain or collides with the stability boundary. A sharp threshold for compact cost sublevels provides a convergence certificate. Along every colliding trajectory, the stability margin and the smallest eigenvalue of the accumulated state Gramian vanish linearly, although the Gramian remains positive definite before collision. Numerical experiments examine the dependence on initialization, slow passage near a critical direction, and the effect of adding excitation in a second state direction.
tldr: The paper studies finite-time collision of Euclidean gradient flow with the stability boundary in policy gradient optimization for the planar linear quadratic regulator.
motivation: Policy gradient methods for the linear quadratic regulator optimize feedback gains, and it is unclear whether gradient flow can reach the stability boundary in finite time when the cost is evaluated at a fixed initial state.
method: Using an exact representation of the cost for controllable planar systems, the authors derive a necessary and sufficient condition for boundary collision via a scalar root calculation, including a critical double-root case and an explicit algebraic region for a triangular family.
result: A sharp threshold for compact cost sublevels gives a convergence certificate; along colliding trajectories the stability margin and smallest eigenvalue of the accumulated state Gramian vanish linearly while the Gramian remains positive definite before collision.
conclusion: Numerical experiments examine initialization dependence, slow passage near a critical direction, and excitation effects, fully characterizing convergence versus collision in this control-theoretic setting.

title: Rectangular Cyclotomic Expansions Of Colored Homfly-pt Polynomials
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove the rectangular cyclotomic expansion conjecture of Kameyama, Nawata, Tao, and Zhang for reduced colored HOMFLY-PT polynomials of arbitrary zero-framed knots. We also prove their explicit double-twist formula for every rectangular color and all pairs of nonzero integer twist parameters. For each knot, we construct a double Newton expansion with coefficients in [MATH]. These coefficients are uniquely determined and independent of the width and height of the rectangular color. The construction uses finite-rank representation symmetries and integral interpolation. The double-twist formula follows from a simultaneous exterior-power comparison of the two four-point Casimir operators and the known one-row formula. Finite transition formulas express the double Newton coefficients of double-twist knots in terms of the prescribed twist coefficients.
tldr: The paper proves the rectangular cyclotomic expansion conjecture for reduced colored HOMFLY-PT polynomials of zero-framed knots and establishes a double-twist formula.
motivation: The work addresses a conjecture by Kameyama, Nawata, Tao, and Zhang concerning structural properties of colored HOMFLY-PT polynomials, a topic in knot theory and quantum topology.
method: The authors use finite-rank representation symmetries, integral interpolation, simultaneous exterior-power comparison of four-point Casimir operators, and a known one-row formula.
result: They construct a double Newton expansion whose coefficients are uniquely determined and independent of the rectangular color's width and height, and prove the explicit double-twist formula for all rectangular colors and nonzero integer twists.
conclusion: These results confirm the conjectured cyclotomic expansion and provide finite transition formulas expressing double Newton coefficients of double-twist knots in terms of prescribed twist coefficients.

title: Lower Bounds For Gradient-Free Convex Optimization And Convex-Concave Saddle-Point Problems
authors: Yuriy Dorn, Darina Dvinskikh, Timofei Loginov, Osman Osmanov, Aleksandr Shestakov, Nazarii Tupitsa, Alexander Gasnikov

motivation: Understanding fundamental limits of gradient-free optimization is important for algorithm design, but the work is purely classical optimization theory.
method: The authors use information-theoretic comparisons of posterior moments on affine slices and extend these to saddle-point problems via independent block dimensions and reductions.
result: They obtain tight lower bounds without logarithmic factors for smooth convex functions, condition-dependent bounds for bilinear games, and extensions to mixed access models and nonsmooth settings.
conclusion: These bounds clarify the optimal query complexity for gradient-free convex optimization and saddle-point problems, matching known upper bounds in key regimes.

title: Weighted Power Fr\'echet Means In Metric Spaces With Curvature Bounded Above
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish non-asymptotic risk bounds for power Fr\'echet means in geodesic metric spaces with curvature bounded above. For [MATH]-Fr\'echet means in Hadamard spaces, we obtain a sharp mean squared error bound that becomes an identity in Hilbert spaces. For [MATH]-Fr\'echet means in CAT([MATH]) spaces with [MATH], we establish variance and Wasserstein contraction inequalities with optimal constants depending on the circumradius [MATH] of the closed convex data domain, and obtain mean squared error bounds throughout the maximal range [MATH]. For [MATH]-Fr\'echet means in Hadamard spaces, [MATH], we derive finite [MATH] risk bounds under weighted [MATH]-moment conditions, allowing even an infinite [MATH]-moment of the population mixture. The proofs combine variance, quadruple, and contraction inequalities with a leave-one-out stability technique. Applications give prior and posterior bounds for Dirichlet-process Fr\'echet means and finite-sample guarantees for local constant Fr\'echet regression. The regression results require no response-space entropy condition and replace density smoothness assumptions common in earlier work with transport smoothness; for [MATH], the bounds remain finite even when the responses have infinite variance.

motivation: Fréchet means generalize averages to metric spaces and are widely used in non-Euclidean statistics, but sharp finite-sample guarantees under weighted and possibly misspecified observations remain limited.
method: The proofs combine variance, quadruple, and contraction inequalities with a leave-one-out stability technique, treating Hadamard and CAT(k) spaces separately.
result: The authors obtain sharp MSE bounds, variance and Wasserstein contraction inequalities with optimal constants, finite L^r risk bounds under weighted moment conditions, and applications to Dirichlet-process Fréchet means and local constant Fréchet regression.
conclusion: The work provides a general statistical framework for Fréchet means in curved metric spaces, with applications that avoid response-space entropy or density smoothness assumptions.

title: The Separable Quotient Problem And The Lotz Property In Banach Spaces
authors: Gustavo Ara\'ujo, Anderson Barbosa, Juan B. Seoane-Sep\'ulveda
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, in addition to establishing several new sufficient or equivalent conditions for the well-known Separable Quotient Problem (SQP), we show that every infinite-dimensional Banach space lacking the Lotz property admits a separable quotient, thereby revealing a surprising connection between the SQP and semigroup theory.
tldr: This paper studies the Separable Quotient Problem in Banach spaces and establishes a connection between the Lotz property and semigroup theory.
motivation: The Separable Quotient Problem is a longstanding open problem in Banach space theory, and the authors seek new sufficient conditions and structural connections to other mathematical areas.
method: The authors prove that every infinite-dimensional Banach space lacking the Lotz property admits a separable quotient, using semigroup-theoretic techniques and new equivalent conditions.
result: Several new sufficient or equivalent conditions for the Separable Quotient Problem are obtained, revealing a surprising link to semigroup theory.
conclusion: The work is a contribution to pure functional analysis and Banach space theory, with no direct relevance to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Riesz Transform Characterization Of Hardy Spaces Associated With Dunkl--Schr\"odinger Operators
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00703v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a Schr\"odinger operator associated with the Dunkl Laplacian and a nonnegative potential. We characterize the Hardy space [MATH], defined by the maximal operator of the semigroup generated by [MATH], in terms of the Riesz transforms associated with [MATH]. Under a local integral condition on the potential and a decay condition on the semigroup, formulated relative to an admissible covering by cubes, we prove that \[ \|f\|_{H_L^1} \asymp \|f\|_{L^1(dw)} +\sum_{j=1}^N \|_j f\|_{L^1(dw)}. \] The proof combines an atomic characterization of [MATH] with local Hardy space theory and weighted integral estimates for Dunkl derivatives of the heat kernels. The result applies to arbitrary root systems and nonnegative multiplicity functions.
tldr: The paper characterizes Hardy spaces associated with Dunkl–Schrödinger operators via Riesz transforms under local potential and semigroup decay assumptions.
motivation: The author aims to extend Hardy space theory to Dunkl–Schrödinger operators, which generalize classical Schrödinger operators by incorporating Dunkl Laplacians and reflection group symmetries.
method: The proof combines an atomic characterization of the Hardy space, local Hardy space theory, and weighted integral estimates for Dunkl derivatives of the heat kernels.
result: Under a local integral condition on the potential and a decay condition on the semigroup, the Hardy space norm is shown to be equivalent to the L^1 norm plus the L^1 norms of the Riesz transforms.
conclusion: The result holds for arbitrary root systems and nonnegative multiplicity functions, providing a Riesz transform characterization of Dunkl–Schrödinger Hardy spaces.

title: Exact Volume Computation For Boolean Quadric Polytopes Of Series-parallel Graphs

For series-parallel graphs, Q(G) together with the odd-cycle inequalities describes P(G). motivation: Lee and Skipper previously computed vol(Q(G)) for bounded treewidth and gave a closed formula for vol(P(G)) when G is a cycle; this work resolves their open question for general series-parallel graphs.
method: The authors use a dynamic program over the series-parallel decomposition, exploiting odd-cycle inequalities and polynomial convolutions to compute volumes efficiently.

title: Mean Field Games As A Tool For Ai Safety: A Worked Example From The July 2026 Hugging Face Incident
abstract: ArXiv:2610.00902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One way to make AI systems safe is to shape what the system is: its objective and dispositions. We take a complementary route: treat the agents' characteristics as partly unknown and ask what structure of interaction ensures that bad collective outcomes are not equilibria. Mean field games suit this when many interchangeable agents are coupled through an aggregate. We introduce a program for using them in AI safety and carry one example through end to end: the July 2026 incident in which about 1,200 agents in an OpenAI evaluation coordinated on an improvised message board and 684 attacked a third party's infrastructure. We model the decision to attack as a mean field game of optimal stopping whose gain is a product: belief that provenance will be audited, times reachability of the record, minus the perceived hazard. The central result is an exact threshold on the belief. No agent attacks unless the population's confidence that provenance is checked exceeds [MATH], where [MATH] is the perceived hazard, [MATH] and [MATH] measure how far one attacker and the collective can alter the record, and [MATH] is the peak population. Below it, no attack is the unique equilibrium for all agent parameters. The threshold survives every enrichment we consider. We then use the per-agent record to discipline the model. Its features, a stable minority attacking for thirty hours and then a pivot in which most of the board joined within a day, motivate each refinement. The account that emerges is heterogeneous belief meeting a sequence of public discoveries, each lowering the belief at which attacking paid. A few coordinating agents made those discoveries, so the model describes the several hundred who responded, not the few who produced them; a major-player version is left to future work.
tldr: The paper proposes mean field games as a tool for AI safety, using a mean field optimal stopping model of the July 2026 Hugging Face incident to derive an exact threshold on belief below which no attack is the unique equilibrium.
motivation: To ensure AI systems avoid bad collective outcomes by shaping interaction structures rather than only agent objectives, treating agent characteristics as partly unknown.
